10124-aunt-jane-s-nieces-and-uncle-john:
Edith Van Dyne, writing under that pen name, published this girls' adventure novel in 1911. It brings back Patsy, Beth, and Louise, the nieces of the first books, with their kind, rich Uncle John. When worry over Patsy sparks a plan, the party sets out on a motor tour that soon turns into much more.

A small dog called Mumbles, a wonder on wheels, a fast chauffeur, and stops among Native peoples fill the road west. Capture, escape, a fiddler, and a confession add danger and romance to the fun. Readers get a cheerful, old-fashioned tale of friendship, travel, and pluck.
1110-king-john:
King John of England fights France, quarrels with the Pope, and loses his nephew Arthur, whose death stains his reign. William Shakespeare's history play follows John's troubled rule through battles, truces, and betrayals, with the Bastard Philip Faulconbridge as its witty, loyal heart.

John's crown rests on a shaky claim, and his barons drift toward the French prince. The play ends with John's death and his young son Henry's accession. Its verse is early and vigorous, and the Bastard's speeches give it lasting life on stage. The Bastard's wit and John's fall give the play its lasting stage life.
1511-king-john:
Shakespeare's King John follows the troubled reign of John of England, from a room of state at Northampton to the walls of Angiers in France. Bastard Philip Faulconbridge, John's witty kinsman, steals scenes, while Arthur, the young rival prince, becomes a pawn of French and English crowns.

Through sieges, a papal legate, and a king's death by poison, the play weighs legitimacy, loyalty, and the fate of children in adult wars. Its verse is uneven but its best speeches shine. King John is a lesser-known history, rewarding for readers who love Shakespeare's political mind.
18631-the-lady-of-fort-st-john:
Mary Hartwell Catherwood published this historical novel at Boston and New York in 1891 with Houghton, Mifflin and Company. It tells the tragedy of Marie de la Tour at Fort St. John, in what is now New Brunswick. Catherwood, sitting on the height above St. John, says the tale recalls Walter Scott, with reality stranger than fiction.

The story rests on papers about the rival chiefs D'Aulnay and La Tour, two well-born, well-off men whose fights shaped Acadia, then a land covering Nova Scotia and much of Maine. Louis XIII's letter to his governor D'Aulnay shows France meddling from afar. The novel brings early colonial strife to life.
2249-king-john:
John, king of England, faces rebellion at home and war with France over the rival claim of young Arthur. King John moves through sieges, papal excommunication, and shifting alliances as nobles change sides and mothers plead for sons. Shakespeare draws on chronicle history to stage a reign defined by insecure power.

The Bastard Philip Faulconbridge, witty and loyal, emerges as the play's moral center amid the maneuvering. Arthur's fall and John's poisoning close a grim story of ambition without glory. Less famous than the later histories, the play still offers stirring speeches and a bleak view of politics.
30629-chicken-little-jane-on-the-big-joh:
Lily Munsell Ritchie writes Chicken Little Jane on the Big John, copyrighted in 1919 by the Britton Publishing Company of New York. An illustration shows a boy coming halfway across and holding out his hand. Eleven chapters open with Huz and Baby Jill in the pasture, harking back to Centerville, and Chicken Little paying a visit.

Later chapters add a cherry penance, guests arriving, a hunting party, pigs, and a party and picnic. Bread and polliwogs, supper at the captain's, and calico scenes follow. Ritchie writes a warm, funny children's tale of farm, river, and family, centered on a small heroine with a big heart.
35574-seeing-france-with-uncle-john:
Seeing France with Uncle John is a comic travel book by Anne Warner, the author of the Susan Clegg stories. The Century Company published it in New York in 1906, with illustrations by May Wilson Preston. The frontispiece shows the narrator reading a guide-book aloud while her uncle contradicts everything in it.

The book is written as letters home, beginning with a letter to Mama. The party did get off at last, about four in the afternoon, after a day with Uncle John that the writer calls awful. The plates show their progress: a fifteenth-century house at Rouen, the clock, and ruins of which Uncle John approves because there has been no tampering with them. At Gisors they study up, guide-book in hand. Warner makes the tour of France a running battle between the book and the uncle.
40116-edith-and-john:
Edith and John, a story of Pittsburgh by Franklin Farquhar, was copyrighted and published in 1912. Chapter one is called The Wrecked Umbrella in the contents. Fog, smoke, and grime hang over the city of Pittsburgh as the tale opens. A thick blanket of wet air lies soggy over the streets that night.

Rain comes down like gimlets, and the air feels savage to the skin. Streets run sodden and muddy, with dirty streams babbling in the gutters. Lights gleam ghastly through the gloom on that November night in the city. Gleaming forges and ponderous hammers of the mills loom in the murk beyond. Industrial Pittsburgh in its smoke and iron forms the ground of this love story.
40775-expositor-s-bible-the-epistles-of-:
William Alexander wrote on the Epistles of Saint John for The Expositor’s Bible set. Hodder and Stoughton issued the volume in London in eighteen hundred ninety six. W Robertson Nicoll edited the whole series. Each cloth volume in the set sold for seven shillings and sixpence.

The series gave one book of the Bible to one strong voice. Marcus Dods took Genesis and the Gospel of John. A Maclaren took the Psalms and Colossians. Alexander, a bishop, took the three short letters of John. His task was to open their sense line by line for lay readers. Church folk who wanted deep help in plain form bought the set shelf by shelf.
42084-the-central-eskimo-sixth-annual-re:
The Central Eskimo is Franz Boas's ethnography of the peoples of the central Arctic, printed for the Smithsonian Institution's Bureau of Ethnology in its Sixth Annual Report. Boas works tribe by tribe across an enormous map. Baffin Land, the western shore of Hudson Bay, Boothia, and Smith Sound supply the ground.

The tribal survey names the Sikosuilarmiut, the Oqomiut, the Iglulirmiut, the Aivillirmiut, the Netchillirmiut, and many more, with the North Greenlanders last. Then come the arts of life: seal, walrus, and whale hunting, deer and musk ox and bear, and fishing. Manufactures, leather work, boats and sledges follow. Houses, clothing, hair dressing, and tattooing get their chapters, and social and religious life closes the account. It is a founding survey of Inuit life, built from field observation and set down group by group.
46337-the-gospel-of-st-john:
The Gospel of John with critical and explanatory notes is a commentary by Joseph MacRory, professor of sacred scripture and Hebrew at Maynooth College. A Greek motto stands at the front, drawn from the gospel itself, about things written so that readers may believe. MacRory's title names his method in its first line: the text of the fourth gospel, with notes that judge and explain.

A professor's book of this kind serves students of the priesthood and serious lay readers alike. Verse by verse help on hard sayings, old questions of authorship, and points of doctrine is the stock of such notes. MacRory wrote from inside the Irish Catholic college world of his day. The Greek lettering at the head shows the book keeps one foot in the original tongue throughout.
55199-the-true-travels-adventures-and-ob:
Captain John Smith wrote The True Travels, Adventures, and Observations of Captain John Smith. The book covers his course in Europe, Asia, Africa, and America, from 1593 to 1629. It is given to the Earl of Pembroke, the Earl of Lindsey, Lord Hunsdon, and other friends. Smith says a learned keeper of antiquity, Sir Robert Cotton, asked for the book. Cotton had read the General History and found harder hazards elsewhere.

Stage men, Smith says, had acted his fatal tragedies and racked his relations at their pleasure. To prevent all future misprisions, he compiled this true discourse. Envy has taxed him to have writ too much and done too little, he owns. He cannot make a monument for himself, he adds, and leave his partners unburied in the fields. Their lives were spent with his, and their names stand here with his own.
611-prester-john:
John Buchan sets this South African adventure in the days before the Boer War's end. Young David Crawfurd, a Scots clerk, meets a black preacher named John Laputa on a Kirkcaple shore, then finds him again as leader of a rising meant to restore Prester John's empire. Treasure caves, drums at sunset, and a collar of kings mark the plot.

Buchan writes with boyish vigor and period views of race that modern readers will find dated. Captain Arcoll, a wily scout, guides Crawfurd through peril. The novel endures as a classic imperial adventure, brisk, vivid, and full of veld, gold, and faith.
6437-the-splendid-spur-being-memoirs-of-:
Arthur T. Quiller Couch, as Q, edits in modern English the memoirs of John Marvel, servant of Charles I in 1642 to 1643, dated 1897. Marvel, who jilted the Muse's gentle pipe for drum and trumpet, fears her revenge now he must write his adventures at home. On November 29, 1642, a clear, frosty day, the King, Prince of Wales newly recovered from measles, and Princes Rupert and Maurice march back from Reading.

Marvel, then a scholar of Trinity College, Oxford, begins at three o'clock, going for a fencing lesson to Mr. Rob. Drury, whose lodgings stand empty at Ship Street's corner by the Corn Market. Later, snoring like a dozen looms through a hut window over a stream draws him to peep before waking the sleeper. Quiller Couch writes a Civil War romance of a scholar turned soldier, with humour, danger, and a splendid spur to adventure.
75543-an-illustrated-commentary-on-the-g:
Lyman Abbott wrote a commentary, with pictures, on the Gospel according to Saint John, issued at New York in 1879. The book is meant for family use, and for the great body of Christian workers of all churches. He gave it to his father, Jacob Abbott, whose writings had opened the Gospel to countless readers. The son praises the father's life as a clearer showing of its spirit.

Added notes treat the start of John's Gospel, the Incarnation, the Lamb of God, Christ as a talker, and the discourse on the bread of life. Later parts take up the woman taken in sin, the parable of the sheepfold, the raising of Lazarus, the anointing of Jesus, and the Lord's Supper. Abbott wrote in a warm way for lay readers, and his commentaries formed a known series on the New Testament.
8043-the-bible-king-james-version-book-4:
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God: John's Gospel opens with a hymn to Christ as the eternal Word made flesh. From there it follows Jesus through signs and long discourses found nowhere else: water turned to wine, Nicodemus by night. The woman at the well, the raising of Lazarus, and the farewell teaching on the night before the cross. It closes with Thomas touching the risen Lord and confessing, my Lord and my God.

John is the most theological Gospel, concerned less with sequence than with who Jesus is. Its images of light, bread, shepherd, and vine have shaped Christian devotion. In the King James Version, its calm, profound prose makes it the Gospel many readers turn to first for prayer and meditation.
8270-the-world-english-bible-web-john:
John, in the World English Bible, opens as the King James version does, yet in modern prose. In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things were made through him, and in him was life, the light of men, shining in darkness that has not overcome it. A note explains that the word for overcome can also mean comprehended, getting a grip on an enemy to defeat him. Lightly reformatted from ebible. org by Martin Ward, the Gospel follows signs, discourses, and resurrection.

The modern version keeps John's theology luminous, from Nicodemus by night to Thomas's confession. Its notes help readers with difficult Greek words. For prayer and study, John here offers the fourth Gospel's depth in today's English, inviting slow reading of its claims about Word, light, and life.
8289-the-world-english-bible-web-1-john:
Whoever wrote 1 John cared less about argument than about assurance: how can believers know they belong to God? His answers are simple and repeated like a refrain. God is light, God is love, and those who know him keep his commands and love their brothers and sisters. Claims to faith without love are empty, he insists, and love without truth is blind.

Warnings against false teachers and against loving the world run through the letter, alongside comfort for readers who doubt themselves. Its short sentences and plain words make it one of the easiest New Testament books to read, and one of the hardest to live up to. The letter ends with a final guard: keep away from idols.
8831-weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-sp:
Weymouth's John, third edition 1913, begins where no other gospel begins: in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things came into being through him, and in him was life, the light of men, shining in darkness the darkness has not overpowered. John the witness comes to testify to the light, so that all might believe through him, though he himself is not the light.

From that prologue, Weymouth's plain English carries John's signs, discourses, and farewell teachings toward the Passion and resurrection appearances. The gospel's high theology and intimate scenes, Nicodemus, the Samaritan woman, Lazarus, sit side by side in modern speech. Readers who find King James John difficult will gain a clear path into its argument, while students can compare Weymouth's renderings with more literal versions.
8850-weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-sp:
The first letter of John, in Weymouth's modern speech, opens with testimony: that which was from the beginning. Which the writers have listened to, seen with their own eyes. Handled with their hands concerning the Word of Life. The Life was manifested, they declare, and they announce what they have seen and heard so that readers may share fellowship with them. That fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ. They write so that joy may be complete.

The letter that follows turns on light and darkness, love and hate, truth and deceit, and the test that those born of God love one another. Weymouth's plain English keeps the letter's repetitions musical rather than confusing. Readers get the New Testament's great meditation on love as evidence of faith, short enough to read in one sitting and deep enough to return to often.
8851-weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-sp:
The Elder writes to the elect lady and her children in Weymouth's second letter of John, loving them truly. Do all who know the truth, for the truth lives in their hearts and will be with them for ever. Grace, mercy, and peace are wished from God the Father and from Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father, in truth and love. It brings intense joy, the Elder says, to find some of her children living true Christian lives, obeying the command received from the Father.

That command, he stresses, is not new but from the beginning: love one another, and walk in truth while refusing deceivers who deny Christ come in the flesh. The letter is only thirteen verses, and Weymouth's version keeps its household scale: a brief note of encouragement and warning to a small community.
8852-weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-sp:
The Elder writes to his dear friend Gaius in Weymouth's third letter of John, with simple affection: truly I love you. He prays that Gaius may prosper in all respects and enjoy good health, just as his soul already prospers. It brings intense joy, he says, when brethren come bearing witness to Gaius's fidelity to truth, that he lives in obedience to it. No greater joy exists, the Elder adds, than hearing that his children live in truth.

Gaius's faithful behaviour toward brethren, even strangers, earns praise, and the brethren have testified to his love before the church. The letter then contrasts the hospitable with Diotrephes, who loves pre-eminence and refuses workers. Weymouth's version keeps this shortest New Testament note warm and personal. Readers get a glimpse of early Christian hospitality, and of how much a small church's health depended on welcome.
9570-reminiscent-poems-part-3-from-volum:
Part three of volume two of Whittier's works gathers his subjective and reminiscent poems, verses of memory and self. Memories opens the run, picturing a bright girl whose mind wakes like a flower in spring light. The Pumpkin, Forgiveness, My Psalm, and The Barefoot Boy follow, each tied to home, youth, or faith. Whittier writes as an old man looking back on a long life.

The poems blend farm scenes, family love, and Quaker trust, with a tone both tender and firm. Snow-Bound, his best-known fireside poem, belongs to this same vein of memory. A reader gets Whittier's inner life in verse, warm and plain, and a record of what one New England life held dear.
9578-poems-in-wartime-part-4-from-volume:
Part four of volume three of Whittier's works gathers his poems In War Time, written during the Civil War. The part opens with a dedication to Samuel and Harriet Sewall, then moves to Thy Will Be Done, A Word for the Hour, and a hymn on Luther's Ein Feste Burg. Pieces on Fremont, the watchers, and Englishmen follow. At Port Royal, Barbara Frietchie, and Astraea at the Capitol mark the war's course.

Later poems hail emancipation, from a Newburyport hymn to the proclamation's anniversary. Whittier, long an abolitionist, greets freedom with prayer and praise, not triumph alone. A reader gets Civil War verse of faith and hope, written as events broke, by a poet who had waited decades for this hour.
9581-personal-poems-i-part-1-from-volume:
Part one of Whittier's personal poems opens with a lament for Charles B. Storrs and lines on the death of S. Oliver Torrey. Leggett's Monument, Lucy Hooper, and a note to a friend with Woolman's Journal follow. Channing, Daniel Wheeler, and Fredrika Bremer earn salutes, with The Hill-Top and Elliott beside. Ichabod and The Lost Occasion mark political grief.

Later poems in the opening group praise Wordsworth, Kossuth, and an old schoolmaster, before turning to The Cross and William Forster. Whittier ties each name to a cause or a memory. A reader gets the first gallery of his personal verse, warm, plain, and full of friendship.
9582-personal-poems-ii-part-2-from-volum:
Part two of Whittier's personal poems gathers verse addressed to friends, heroes, and public men. The Cross opens, honoring Richard Dillingham, a young Quaker who died in a Nashville jail for aiding runaway slaves. Other poems salute Charles Sumner, Burns, Garibaldi, and Lydia Maria Child, with Brown of Ossawatomie among them. Each piece ties a person to a cause Whittier held dear.

Later poems mark Bryant's birthday, Thomas Starr King, and a welcome to Lowell, blending praise with memory. Whittier's tone stays warm, plain, and earnest throughout. A reader gets a gallery of Whittier's age in verse, and a sense of the friendships that fed his reform life.
9583-occasional-poems-part-3-from-volume:
Part three of Whittier's occasional poems gathers verse for days, places, and friends. Eva opens, drawn from Mrs. Stowe's Uncle Tom's Cabin, when Eva's fate moved firesides across America. A Lay of Old Time, A Song of Harvest, and Kenoza Lake follow, with hymns for church openings and a golden wedding at Longwood. Lexington, The Library, and Centennial Hymn mark public hours.

Later poems salute the Bartholdi Statue, greet friends, and bid godspeed to travelers. Whittier writes for the occasion with warmth and craft. A reader gets a varied set of public and private lyrics, where a poet lent his voice to his age's milestones.
9589-tales-and-sketches-part-3-from-volu:
Part three of Whittier's Tales and Sketches opens with The Little Iron Soldier, or what Aminadab Ivison dreamed about. Aminadab, a portly, easy man, wakes at one in the morning after a night of kicking and threshing in sleep. His wife scolds his restless night, and his dream tale unfolds. Passaconaway, The Opium Eater, and The Proselytes follow in the part.

Other sketches include David Matson, The Fish I Didn't Catch, and Yankee Gypsies, with Patucket Falls and The Lighting Up beside. Whittier mixes humor, legend, and moral point with ease. A reader gets a varied set of his prose tales, where dreams, Indians, and Yankee folk share one fireside.
9593-historical-papers-part-3-from-volum:
Part three of volume six of Whittier's works gathers his historical papers, essays on men and hours of the past. Daniel O'Connell opens, answering Henry Clay's 1839 Senate slur on the great Irish liberator. England under James II, The Border War of 1708, and The Great Ipswich Fright follow. The Boy Captives and Black Men in the Revolution and War of 1812 add American scenes.

Later papers treat the Scottish reformers, the Pilgrims of Plymouth, Governor Endicott, and John Winthrop. Whittier writes as a moral historian, praising freedom's friends. A reader gets compact, earnest history essays, rich in New England and Irish memory.
aunt-jane-s-nieces-and-uncle-john:
Edith Van Dyne, L. Frank Baum's series pen name, published this third nieces volume in 1911. Uncle John takes Beth, Patsy, and a new protegee, crippled Myrtle Dean, on a motor tour through the American West. Major Gregory Doyle paces the sitting room in the opening chapter, sure something has happened to Patsy, beside a dog called Mumbles.

Their car, a wonder on wheels, speeds behind the chauffeur Wampus through Indian country and coyote-haunted nights. Chapters promise a real adventure at last: capture, a fiddler, an escape, and the romance of Dan'l. Horsemen hail the travellers with a bantering welcome to Hades on the road. Point Loma ends the route, after confessions and tales of woe have sorted every passenger's past.
britannica-1911-abercrombie-john:
John Abercrombie receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abercrombie, a Scottish physician born at Aberdeen in 1780, took his M.D. at Edinburgh in 1803 and rose fast in practice there. A minister's son, he led the city's medicine within years.

Journal papers from 1816 grew into two 1828 books: one on diseases of the brain and spinal cord, one on the intestinal canal, liver, and abdominal viscera. Thought drew him too: Inquiries concerning the Intellectual Powers in 1830 and The Philosophy of the Moral Feelings in 1833 sold widely. The entry grants them little novelty yet wide popularity. He died at Edinburgh in November 1844, his name fixed in medical teaching of the day.
britannica-1911-adair-john:
John Adair (died 1722) was a Scottish surveyor and map-maker. Nothing is known of his parentage or early life. His name reached the public in 1683. A prospectus for a Scottish Atlas appeared at Edinburgh. It announced his appointment by the Privy Council. He was to survey the shires of Scotland. Parliament passed tonnage acts in his favour. Coastal survey work followed from that support. The Royal Society made him a fellow in 1688.

Money troubles shadow the achievement. In 1703 he published the first part of his coastal description. The second part never appeared at all. He likely lost considerable money on the work. Government paid his widow some remuneration in 1723. His surviving work rests in Edinburgh and London libraries. Seamen were its intended users throughout.
britannica-1911-adams-john:
John Adams (1735-1826) was the second president of the United States. He was born in October 1735 at Quincy, Massachusetts. His father was a farmer of Devonshire descent. Harvard graduated young Adams in 1755. He taught school at Worcester briefly. Law study under Rufus Putnam followed there. The bar admitted him in 1758. James Otis's writs-of-assistance argument fired him in 1761. Constitutional law became his revolutionary weapon.

Influence grew through the Stamp Act crisis. Adams drafted Braintree's instructions in 1765. Other towns copied them as models widely. The peace negotiations show his stubborn independence. He and Jay outvoted Franklin in Paris. They dealt directly with Britain, ignoring French instructions. Fisheries rights were his particular demand. Abigail Adams, his wife, left letters of great value.
britannica-1911-aikin-john:
Aikin, John, an English doctor and writer of 1747 to 1822, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Kibworth-Harcourt, he was educated at the Nonconformist academy at Warrington, where his father taught. He studied medicine at Edinburgh and in London under William Hunter, then practised as a surgeon at Chester and Warrington. A Leyden doctorate in 1780 led to practice at Yarmouth and later London.

Writing soon mattered more to him than medicine, along with defending liberty of conscience. With his sister, Mrs Barbauld, he produced Evenings at Home, six volumes of family reading translated into almost every European language. He edited the Monthly Magazine for a decade and ran a paper called the Athenaeum. His large General Biography ran to ten volumes, and his daughter Lucy Aikin also won a name as a historian.
britannica-1911-aislabie-john:
Aislabie, John, an English politician of 1670 to 1742, is given his own article within the hosted text of the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Goodramgate, York, he was the fourth son of the principal registrar of York's archiepiscopal court. He entered parliament in 1695 as member for Ripon. Office followed: admiralty commissioner, treasurer of the navy, and privy councillor.

In March 1718 Aislabie became chancellor of the exchequer, the crown's chief finance officer. He pushed the South Sea Company's plan to pay off the national debt through the Commons. When the company collapsed, a secret inquiry declared him guilty of promoting the scheme for his own exorbitant profit. He was expelled from the House and briefly held in the Tower. Released, he kept the property he had owned before 1718 and retired to his country estate.
britannica-1911-alcock-john:
John Alcock (about 1430–1500) rose fast in both church and state after being made dean of Westminster in 1461. Born at Beverley in Yorkshire and schooled at Cambridge, the English churchman became master of the rolls in 1462, then went to Castile as envoy in 1470.

Rochester made him its bishop in 1472; Worcester followed in 1476 and Ely in 1486. Twice he served as lord chancellor, and he showed real skill in talks with James III of Scotland. He ranks among the top churchmen of the years before the Reformation, a man of deep learning who also knew building well. At Beverley he set up a charity; at Hull, a grammar school; and many churches owe him their repair. His grandest work was to found Jesus College, Cambridge, on the grounds of St Radigund's convent.
britannica-1911-alden-john:
Alden, John, one of the Mayflower Pilgrims, who lived from about 1599 to 1687, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Bradford's history of Plymouth Plantation says he was hired as a cooper, a barrel-maker, at Southampton where the ship took on supplies. Bradford calls him a hopeful young man who was much desired. He sailed in 1620 and helped found the Plymouth Colony.

Alden settled early at Duxbury, Massachusetts, and lived there most of his life. From 1633 to 1675 he served as an Assistant to the colony's governor, often acting as governor himself. At his death in September 1687 he was the last male survivor among the signers of the Mayflower Compact. Popular memory keeps him for a different reason: Longfellow's poem The Courtship of Miles Standish tells how he wooed Priscilla Mullins for his friend Standish, then married her himself in 1623.
britannica-1911-allen-john:
John Allen (1476–1534) was an English churchman who studied at both Oxford and Cambridge. Archbishop Warham sent him on a church mission to Rome. On his return he held a string of livings, and in 1516 became rector of South Ockenden in Essex. He also held a prebend at Lincoln Cathedral. In the closing of the lesser monasteries in 1524 and 1525 he gave Wolsey much help.

Allen gained prebends at Nottingham in 1526 and at St Paul's in London in 1527. He gave both up in 1528 on his choice as archbishop of Dublin. For four years he was chancellor of Ireland, but his career was full of strife. In 1531 he was fined under the laws of Provisors and Praemunire. In 1534 he met a violent death at the hands of men who followed Lord Thomas Fitzgerald.
britannica-1911-almon-john:
John Almon (1737–1805) was an English political pamphleteer and publisher, born at Liverpool on 17 December 1737. Apprenticed to a printer in his native town, he also spent two years at sea before coming to London in 1758. His own early publications on political subjects won great if brief popularity and brought him to the notice of the Whig opposition's leaders.

The Whigs, harassed by government, badly needed a channel to the public, and Almon supplied it. In 1763 he opened a bookseller's shop in Piccadilly devoted to political pamphlets, accepting real personal risk from prosecutions. The entry credits him with doing much to secure freedom of the press. He later published an edition of Junius and, in his last work, Wilkes's correspondence with a memoir. His anonymous writings, it concludes, matter more as evidence for political history than as literature.
britannica-1911-arbuthnot-john:
John Arbuthnot (1667–1735) was a British physician and author. He was born at Arbuthnott in Kincardineshire. His father was an episcopalian minister there. That father lost his living in 1689. Refusal to conform to Presbyterianism caused it. John went to London in 1691. He supported himself teaching mathematics there. A learned linen-draper housed him kindly.

His first book treated the laws of chance. It drew on Huygens's Dutch treatise. Oxford admitted him as fellow-commoner in 1692. St Andrews granted his medical degree in 1696. He confuted Woodward's deluge theory in 1697. The Royal Society elected him in 1704. Chance brought him to Prince George's sickbed at Epsom. Queen Anne made him physician extraordinary in 1705. Royal physician followed four years later. Aitken's 1892 life anchors the references.
britannica-1911-ashburnham-john:
John Ashburnham (c. 1603–1671) was an English royalist, son of Sir John Ashburnham of Ashburnham in Sussex. He entered the king's service at a young age. In 1627 his kin, the duke of Buckingham, sent him to Paris to sound out terms for peace. In 1628 he made ready to join the force for Rochelle, a plan cut short by the duke's death by a killer's hand. That year he became a groom of the bedchamber and a member of parliament for Hastings.

Ashburnham also sat for Hastings in the Long Parliament of 1640. In that place he served the king by reports of what was said and done. He made a large wealth and won back the family estates his father had lost. He became one of the king's chief men of trust.
britannica-1911-aubrey-john:
Aubrey, John is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an English collector of old lore and lives. John Aubrey was born near Malmesbury in Wiltshire on the twelfth of March 1626 and died in 1697. His father was a country gentleman of good means. At school, in his master's house, the boy first met the thinker Thomas Hobbes, about whom he would leave many choice tales.

He entered Trinity College, Oxford, in 1642, but the Civil War broke up his studies. In 1649 he brought the great stone rings at Avebury to men's notice. His father died in 1652, leaving him large estates and, with them, tangled lawsuits. The article shows a man who lived gladly and spent his means on the company of famed men and on all he could learn of them. His short lives of his peers remain his mark.
britannica-1911-austin-john:
John Austin is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of an English jurist. He lived from 1790 to 1859. He was born on the third of March 1790. His father owned flour mills at Ipswich and near by. John was the eldest of five brothers in all. John entered the army at a very early age.

He is said to have been only sixteen then. He served under Lord William Bentinck in Malta and Sicily. He seems to have liked his profession well enough. He joined in the amusements of his brother officers. Yet a journal kept by him shows a serious bent. He spent time on studies rare among young officers. In one year he read works of Dugald Stewart. He also read histories of philosophy and of Greece. The entry traces a mind already turning to deep questions.
britannica-1911-aylmer-john:
Aylmer, John (1521-1594), was an English churchman born at Tivetshall St Mary in Norfolk, whose quickness as a boy won him schooling at Cambridge from the marquis of Dorset. About 1541 he became chaplain to Dorset and tutor to his daughter, Lady Jane Grey.

Opposition to transubstantiation in convocation cost Aylmer his archdeaconry. It drove him into exile in Switzerland. There he answered Knox's Blast against women rulers. He also helped Foxe turn the Acts of the Martyrs into Latin. Elizabeth's accession brought him home, to archdeaconries and, in 1576, the bishopric of London. There his harsh rule over Puritans and Papists alike made him notorious, mocked in the Marprelate Tracts and in Spenser's verse as Morrell, the bad shepherd.
britannica-1911-bacon-john:
Bacon, John (1740-1799), was a British sculptor born in Southwark, son of a cloth-worker, and apprenticed at fourteen to a Lambeth porcelain works. Painting small china ornaments first, he soon stood out as a modeller, and watching fine sculptors' models sent to a neighbouring pottery for firing fixed his ambition.

Bacon improved work in artificial stone and invented a better pointing instrument for transferring a model's form to marble exactly. Prizes followed: a figure of Peace won in 1758, the Royal Academy's first gold medal for sculpture in 1769, and a Mars that made him an associate in 1770. A bust of George III for Christ Church, Oxford, won the king's lasting favor, though rival sculptors charged him with ignorance of classic style.
britannica-1911-baconthorpe-john:
Baconthorpe, John (d. 1346), called the Resolute Doctor, was a learned Carmelite monk born at Baconthorpe in Norfolk, possibly a grandnephew of Roger Bacon. Raised in the Blakeney monastery near Walsingham, he studied at Oxford and Paris, where he was known as a Princeps, a leading figure, among the Averroists.

In 1329 Baconthorpe became twelfth provincial of the English Carmelites. He is said to have foreshadowed Wycliffe in urging that clergy stand under the king, and at Rome in 1333 he first upheld, then retracted, papal authority in divorce cases. His chief work was a commentary on the four books of the Sentences. It was printed in 1510. Padua still studied it nearly three centuries later. The thinker Vanini spoke of him with great respect.
britannica-1911-badby-john:
Badby, John (d. 1410), was one of the early Lollard martyrs, a tailor, or perhaps a blacksmith, from the west Midlands of England. The Worcester church court condemned him for denying transubstantiation, the teaching that the consecrated bread becomes Christ's body.

Badby held bluntly that Christ at supper had not held his own body in his hand, and that if every consecrated host were the Lord's body, England would hold 20,000 gods. A second court under Archbishop Arundel at St Paul's sent him to burn at Smithfield. The prince of Wales, the future Henry V, watched and offered him life and a pension to recant; he refused, and died in the fire.
britannica-1911-bainbridge-john:
Bainbridge, John (1582-1643), was an English astronomer from Ashby-de-la-Zouch. He began as a physician. He practised medicine for some years. He also kept a school and studied astronomy. In London he joined the college of physicians in 1618.

A pamphlet on the comet of 1618 brought Bainbridge notice. Sir Henry Savile had just founded an astronomy chair at Oxford. He gave Bainbridge that chair in 1619. Bainbridge joined Merton College there. He later read Linacre's medical lectures as well. He died at Oxford in 1643. His works include a description of the late comet. He also translated Proclus on the sphere. He turned Ptolemy's work on planetary theories into English. Manuscripts of his survive at Trinity College, Dublin.
britannica-1911-bale-john:
John Bale (1495–1563) was an English author and bishop of Ossory, born at Cove in Suffolk. At twelve he entered the Carmelite house at Norwich, then went to Jesus College, Cambridge, taking his degree in 1529. At Cambridge he fell under the sway of the reformers and gave up his monastic life.

Bale married, took a parish, and was soon hauled before church courts for his preaching. Thomas Cromwell shielded him, drawn, it was said, by his miracle plays. The 1911 Britannica entry paints a fierce controversialist whose plays spared no decency in attacking monks and their backers, with a sample prayer from his Thre Laws quoted as proof.
britannica-1911-balguy-john:
John Balguy (1686–1748) was an English divine and philosopher, born at Sheffield on 12 August 1686. He studied at St John's College, Cambridge, was ordained in 1710, and took a small living in Durham the next year. Writing as Silvius, he entered print backing Bishop Hoadley in the Bangorian controversy.

Moral questions fill his later books. In 1726 he argued that love of virtue for its own sake is the highest moral rule, while rewards and punishments still help uphold conduct. The 1911 Britannica entry then sets out his Foundation of Moral Goodness. That work opposed Hutcheson's view. It held, with Cudworth and Clarke, that virtue means acting by reason and by fixed relations among things.
britannica-1911-ballance-john:
John Ballance (1839–1893) was a New Zealand statesman, born on 27 March 1839 at Glenavy in County Antrim. Trained in a national school and apprenticed to an ironmonger, he worked as a clerk in Birmingham before sailing for New Zealand. At Wanganui he founded the Wanganui Herald and stayed its chief owner for life.

During the fighting with the Maori chief Titokowaru in 1867, Ballance helped raise a troop of horse. He won the New Zealand war medal. Yet he lost his commission over critical articles in his own paper. He entered the colony's parliament in 1875. The 1911 Britannica entry traces his service in three ministries. In the last of them he was himself premier, from 1891 to 1893.
britannica-1911-bampton-john:
John Bampton (about 1690–1751) was an English divine, a member of Trinity College, Oxford, who took his master's degree in 1712 and later held a canonry at Salisbury. He died on 2 June 1751, aged sixty-one. The 1911 Britannica entry is not about his ministry but about what his will set up.

His will ordered eight lectures each year at Oxford, in the University Church, on set Sunday mornings in term. Their themes were fixed: to confirm the Christian faith, to refute heretics, and to uphold the authority of Scripture, the early fathers, and the creeds. The lecturer must hold a master's degree from Oxford or Cambridge, and no one may serve twice. The lectures began in 1780 and still went on.
britannica-1911-banim-john:
John Banim (1798–1842) was an Irish novelist, sometimes called the Scott of Ireland, born at Kilkenny on 3 April 1798. At thirteen he entered Kilkenny College and gave himself to drawing and painting, then studied two years in Dublin and taught drawing at home. There he fell in love with a pupil whose parents removed her; she died within two months.

Her death marked Banim's health for good. Settled in Dublin in 1820, he turned to literature, printed a poem, and saw his play Damon and Pythias staged at Covent Garden in 1821. With his elder brother Michael he planned tales of Irish life to do for Ireland what Scott's Waverley novels did for Scotland. The 1911 Britannica entry follows his London years of magazine and stage work.
britannica-1911-barnard-john:
John Barnard was an English musician, a minor canon of St Paul's Cathedral in the reign of Charles I. He holds one clear first: he was the first to publish a collection of English cathedral music. That single fact fills most of this short entry.

His collection holds some of the finest masterpieces of the 1500s, ranging from the faux-bourdon style of Tallis's Pieces and Responses to the most developed types of the full anthem. One caution is added by the 1911 Britannica entry: the text of his book is not trustworthy. Readers get the scope of the collection, from simple chant harmony to grand anthems, and that warning, and little more.
britannica-1911-barnardo-thomas-john:
Thomas John Barnardo (1845–1905) was an English philanthropist, founder of homes for destitute children, born at Dublin in 1845 of a Spanish father and an English mother. He studied medicine at the London Hospital, then at Paris and Edinburgh, meaning to qualify for medical missionary work in China, and became a fellow of the Royal College of Surgeons.

Medical work in London's east end during the cholera epidemic of 1865 showed him the crowds of homeless children in England's cities. Backed by Lord Shaftesbury and Earl Cairns, he gave up China. The first Dr Barnardo's Home opened in 1867 at Stepney Causeway. By his death in 1905 the work had grown to 112 district homes across the United Kingdom, the 1911 Britannica entry records.
britannica-1911-barnett-john:
John Barnett (1802–1890) was an English musical composer, born at Bedford, son of a Prussian jeweller who had changed his name from Bernhard Beer on settling in England. At eleven Barnett sang on the Lyceum stage in London. His fine voice earned him a musical education, and he soon began writing songs and light pieces for the stage.

His Mountain Sylph, produced at the Lyceum on 25 August 1834, won a warm welcome as the first modern English opera, and two more operas followed. Later he taught singing at Cheltenham and printed books on singing method. The 1911 Britannica entry adds his nephew John Francis Barnett, a pianist and composer who studied in Germany and played at the Leipzig Gewandhaus in 1860.
britannica-1911-barrow-sir-john:
Sir John Barrow (1764–1848), an English official and travel writer born at Dragley Beck in Lancashire, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography. He began as a foundry clerk and a mathematics teacher at Greenwich. Through Sir George Staunton he joined the first British embassy to China as comptroller of Lord Macartney's household, learned Chinese well, and later wrote on China for the Quarterly Review.

South Africa and the Admiralty fill the rest of his career. Barrow travelled through the Cape Colony in 1797 reporting on its interior and its peoples, then settled briefly in Cape Town. Back in England, he served as second secretary to the Admiralty for forty years under eleven chief lords. Knighted by a baronetcy in 1835, he retired in 1845, promoted Arctic exploration in print, and wrote travels and lives of Macartney, Anson, and Howe.
britannica-1911-bartholomew-john:
John Bartholomew (1831–1893), a Scottish cartographer born in Edinburgh on Christmas Day 1831, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His father ran a map-making business in Edinburgh, and the son was educated in that work. He then assisted the German geographer August Petermann before taking over the family firm in 1856, the house that became known as the Edinburgh Geographical Institute.

Maps of Britain are the entry's main praise. Under Bartholomew the firm gained a reputation in Britain for fine cartographical work that the entry calls unsurpassed. Special mention goes to maps reduced from the Ordnance Survey, with relief shown by contour lines and a systematic scale of colours. The half-inch series, later extended by his son and successor John George Bartholomew, is called the finest of its kind ever produced. John Bartholomew died in London in March 1893.
britannica-1911-bartlett-john:
John Bartlett (1820–1905), an American publisher and compiler born in Plymouth, Massachusetts, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He became a bookseller and publisher in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and from 1865 to 1889 he was a partner in the Boston firm of Little, Brown and Company. Reference books, patiently assembled over years, were the work that made his name known far beyond the book trade of New England.

Two books dominate the entry. Familiar Quotations, first published in 1855 and greatly expanded later, became the best-known collection of its kind. Then in 1894, after many years of labour, Bartlett issued a complete concordance to Shakespeare's plays, with a supplement for the poems, fuller in its citations than any before it. The entry credits his wife, a Harvard professor's daughter, with great help in all his work. He died at Cambridge in December 1905.
britannica-1911-bascom-john:
John Bascom (1827– ), an American educationalist and writer on philosophy, born at Genoa, New York, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He graduated at Williams College in 1849 and at Andover Theological Seminary in 1855. That same year he became professor of rhetoric at Williams, a post he held until 1874. He then led the University of Wisconsin as its president, teaching mental and moral philosophy there until 1887.

Later years brought Bascom back to Williams. He lectured in sociology, taught economics there through the 1890s, and retired in 1903. The entry lists a long shelf of his books rather than describing any one of them. Titles run from Aesthetics and Philosophy of Rhetoric through Science, Philosophy and Religion. Later books include Problems in Philosophy, The New Theology, Social Theory, and Evolution and Religion, ending with God and His Goodness in 1901. Together they map a career spent joining philosophy, religion, and social questions.
britannica-1911-baskerville-john:
John Baskerville (1706–1775), an English printer born at Wolverley in Worcestershire, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He became a writing master at Birmingham around 1726, showing great talent for calligraphy and for cutting inscriptions in stone. At Birmingham he improved japanning, coating objects with a hard varnish finish, and made a fortune from it. Only then did he turn seriously to printing and type.

Type made Baskerville's lasting name. From about 1750 he experimented in type-founding and produced letters much clearer and more elegant than those then in use. His first book, a Virgil in 1757, was followed by a famous Milton in 1758. He was then made printer to Cambridge University, with editions of the Bible and the Prayer Book. His Horace of 1762 is singled out for correctness and for the beauty of its paper and type. His widow Sarah carried on the business after his death in January 1775.
britannica-1911-bastwick-john:
John Bastwick (1593–1654), an English physician and religious controversialist born at Writtle in Essex, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Briefly educated at Cambridge, he wandered on the Continent and graduated in medicine at Padua before settling at Colchester. His fame rests on fierce opposition to Roman Catholic ceremonial. Around 1633 he printed two Latin treatises in Holland against papal religion and its bishops, and Archbishop Laud's party took them as aimed at England's own prelates.

Punishment made Bastwick a public martyr. The court of high commission fined him £1000, excommunicated him, banned him from practice, and burned his books. He answered with more attacks, calling the bishops enemies of God. Tried alongside Prynne and Burton, he was fined £5000, pilloried, cropped of his ears, and sent to lifelong prison in Scilly. Parliament reversed the sentence in 1640 and voted him £5000 in reparation. He later served in the parliamentary army.
britannica-1911-bates-john:
John Bates is the name at the heart of a famed case in English law, tried in November 1606 and set out in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Bates, a merchant of the Levant Company, refused to pay an extra duty of five shillings per hundredweight on imported currants. The crown had laid that tax by its own power alone, on top of the duty granted by parliament. Bates held it was not lawful without parliament's consent.

Judgment went to the crown, and that was the danger. All four barons of the court of exchequer backed the king. Chief Baron Fleming split the king's power in two: an ordinary power bound by common law, and an absolute power for the common good. Baron Clark added that a past act could not bind the king's heirs. The ruling threatened to free the king from parliament as trade grew.
britannica-1911-beaumont-sir-john:
John Beaumont is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Beaumont was an English poet born in Leicestershire in 1583. His father was a judge, and the playwright Francis Beaumont was his younger brother. Deaths in the family made John head of the house while still young. He went to Oxford and then read law in London.

The article notes his first long poem, on tobacco, printed in 1602 when he was nineteen. It was written in smooth verse pairs. He lived for years on his estates and wrote a long sacred poem now lost. Late in life he went to court and was made a baronet in 1626. He died the next year. His son later printed his poems, by which his name now stands.
britannica-1911-bellenden-john:
John Bellenden (flourished 1533–1587), also written Ballantyne or Bannatyne, was a Scottish writer of the south-east. He studied at St Andrews and at Paris, where he took a doctor’s degree. From his youth he served James V as clerk of accounts at the Scottish court.

At the king’s wish Bellenden turned Boece’s Latin history of Scotland and the first five books of Livy into Scots prose, finishing in 1533. The work won him the posts of archdeacon of Moray and canon of Ross. His Boece, printed in 1536, stands as a strong, free piece of early Scottish prose. A firm foe of the Reformation, he was driven into exile.
britannica-1911-benbow-john:
John Benbow (1653–1702) was an English admiral, son of a Shrewsbury tanner, who went to sea very young. He served in the navy, then traded in his own ship and beat off a Salli pirate in the Mediterranean in 1686. Under William III he rose fast, bombarded St Malo and blockaded Dunkirk.

Sent to the West Indies in 1701 as commander-in-chief, Benbow chased four French ships near Santa Marta in August 1702 with seven of his own. His captains mutinied in all but name and left his flagship unsupported. A chain-shot shattered his right leg, yet he stayed on deck till morning before giving up the chase. He died of his wounds at Jamaica that November.
britannica-1911-bennett-john:
John Bennett was an English madrigal composer, counted among the finest of his school. His first set of madrigals came out in 1599. When Ravenscroft printed five more of them in a collection of 1614, his praise of Bennett reads like an obituary notice.

The Musical Antiquarian Society reprinted that first set in 1845, keeping the music in reach. Beyond the set, Bennett’s work amounts to pieces in the Triumphs of Oriana and in collections of church music. No dates for his birth or death are given at all. What survives is the standing of the madrigals themselves, and the eulogy of a fellow musician who plainly thought him gone by 1614.
britannica-1911-beresford-john:
John Beresford (1738–1805) was an Irish statesman, younger son of Sir Marcus Beresford, earl of Tyrone. Powerful family ties stood behind him from birth. Trinity College, Dublin, the Irish bar, and a Waterford seat in the Irish parliament in 1760 opened his career.

Industry carried Beresford to the privy council in 1768 and the revenue board in 1770. As first commissioner of revenue from 1780 he held great sway in Ireland’s government. He reformed the tax machinery and improved Dublin’s public buildings and streets. His clash with Grattan’s party came in 1784 over trade terms with England, and he later helped settle the money relations of the Union before leaving office in 1802.
britannica-1911-berry-john:
John, Duke of Berry (1340–1416), was the third son of King John II of France. He was born at Vincennes on 30 November 1340. In 1356 he became count of Poitiers. He went to England in 1360 as a hostage for the Treaty of Bretigny. He came home in 1367 to collect his ransom. Berry and Auvergne were granted to him as fiefs.

The 1911 Britannica entry stresses his taste over his war record. He took no lead in the English wars. His energy went to art and luxury instead. He held Languedoc and crushed its peasant revolts with harshness. He built palaces at Poitiers, Bourges, and Paris. At his death he left vast jewels, art, and illuminated manuscripts.
britannica-1911-biddle-john:
John Biddle (1615–1662) is often called the father of English Unitarianism. He was born at Wotton-under-Edge in Gloucestershire. He studied at the town grammar school and at Magdalen Hall, Oxford. He took his master's degree in 1641. He then became master of the free school at Gloucester. His private theology studies soon brought trouble on him.

A friend betrayed his manuscript Twelve Arguments against the deity of the Holy Spirit. In December 1645 a parliamentary committee jailed him, though he lay sick with fever. The 1911 Britannica entry follows years of summonses, trials, and bans that followed. Cromwell sent him to the Scilly Islands in 1655, with 100 crowns a year. Freed in 1658, he was arrested again in London in 1662. He died of fever in prison that September.
britannica-1911-bigelow-john:
John Bigelow (1817– ) was an American journalist and diplomat, born at Malden, New York. He graduated at Union College in 1835 and practised law in New York. He then turned to journalism. With William Cullen Bryant he owned and edited the New York Evening Post from 1849 to 1861. He went to Paris as United States consul in 1861. He rose to minister to France in 1864.

His Paris years hold the heart of the 1911 Britannica entry. He found a French shipbuilder secretly building ironclads and corvettes for the Confederacy. With Napoleon III's connivance behind the scheme, Bigelow worked to block delivery. He stopped all but one vessel reaching Confederate agents. He told that story in France and the Confederate Navy in 1888. Later he edited Franklin's works and wrote lives of Bryant and Tilden.
britannica-1911-bona-john:
John Bona (1609–1674) was an Italian cardinal known for writings on worship and the devout life. Born at Mondovi in Piedmont on 10 October 1609, he joined the Congregation of Feuillants in 1624. He rose in his order as prior of Asti, abbot of Mondovi, and at last its general.

Clement IX made him cardinal in 1669, and at the conclave after that pope's death he was thought a possible pope himself. He died on 27 October 1674. His books deal chiefly with liturgy, the rules of services, and devotion, and they are praised for their store of rubrical detail. The best editions named are Paris (1677), Turin (1747), and Antwerp (1777).
britannica-1911-bright-john:
John Bright (1811–1889) was a British statesman born at Rochdale on 16 November 1811. His father Jacob Bright, a respected Quaker who started a cotton mill at Rochdale in 1809, had come from Coventry stock that traced back to a Wiltshire yeoman. John was the second of eleven children of Jacob's second marriage, and by an elder brother's death became the eldest son.

A delicate child, he was schooled close to home, then at the Quaker school at Ackworth, two years at York and a year and a half at Newton near Clitheroe. He himself said he learned little Latin and Greek through that schooling. The long life that follows traces the mill owner's son into Parliament and national fame. Family roots, Quaker schooling and Rochdale trade are set out first. The rise thus rests on firm ground.
britannica-1911-britton-john:
John Britton (1771–1857) was an English antiquary born on 7 July 1771 at Kington-St-Michael near Chippenham to parents in humble circumstances. Orphaned young, he went to London at sixteen as apprentice to a wine merchant. Ill health cut the term short and left him adrift without money or friends, working strange shifts to live.

Cellarman at a tavern, clerk to a lawyer, singer and reciter at a small theatre, compiler of common songs: the list shows his scramble. A Salisbury publisher's commission for an account of Wiltshire turned his luck. With Edward Wedlake Brayley he produced The Beauties of Wiltshire in 1801, first of the Beauties of England and Wales series. Digby Wyatt credits him with creating popular topography as a kind of book. His Architectural Antiquities ran to nine volumes from 1805 to 1814 and Cathedral Antiquities to fourteen from 1814 to 1835.
britannica-1911-broderip-william-john:
William John Broderip (1789–1859) was an English naturalist born in Bristol on 21 November 1789 who spent his working life in the law. After graduating at Oxford he was called to the bar in 1817 and worked some years at law reporting. In 1822 he became a metropolitan police magistrate, holding the office until 1856 at the Thames court and then at Westminster.

His leisure went to natural history, and his writings did much to push the study of zoology in England. He wrote the zoological articles in the Penny Cyclopaedia, and pieces for Fraser's Magazine were gathered in 1848 as Zoological Recreations, followed in 1852 by Leaves from the Note-book of a Naturalist. He helped found the Zoological Society of London, and the great shell collection he formed was bought in the end by the British Museum. He died in London on 27 February 1859.
britannica-1911-buckeridge-john:
John Buckeridge (c. 1562–1631) was an English divine. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his career in the church. He was educated at the Merchant Taylors school. He then went to St John's College, Oxford. He became a fellow of that college. At Oxford he tutored the young William Laud. His teaching may well have shaped Laud's views.

King James I held Buckeridge in high esteem. He made him a royal chaplain. In 1605 Buckeridge became president of St John's College. He left that post to become bishop of Rochester in 1611. In 1628 he moved to the bishopric of Ely. He died on 23 May 1631. He won some fame as a theologian. He also wrote as a controversialist, defending church positions. He was a close friend of Bishop Lancelot Andrewes. With Laud, he published Andrewes' Ninety-one Sermons in 1629.
britannica-1911-burgoyne-john:
John Burgoyne is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Burgoyne was an English general and playwright who lived from 1722 to 1792. He entered the army young and made a runaway marriage with a lord's daughter. Debts forced him to sell his post, and he lived abroad for seven years. His wife's family then helped restore him to the army.

The article follows his service in raids on the French coast and his part in forming light cavalry units. He won praise in Portugal by taking two towns. He sat in parliament and attacked Lord Clive in sharp speeches. He also wrote plays and gambled heavily. In 1777 he led an invasion of the American colonies from Canada. Cut off at Saratoga, he surrendered his whole force. That loss proved the turning point of the war.
britannica-1911-burns-john:
Burns, John is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an English labour politician. John Burns was born at Vauxhall, London, in October 1858, the second son of an engineer from Ayrshire. He went to school in Battersea until he was ten. Then he was sent to work in a candle factory. At fourteen he was bound for seven years to an engineer at Millbank.

He kept up his schooling at night and read widely, above all Owen, Mill, Paine, and Cobbett. A French workmate who had seen the Paris Commune taught him socialist ideas at first hand. After work at his trade across England and on shipboard, he spent a year on the West African coast as a foreman engineer. The entry traces a self-made path from the work bench to public life.
britannica-1911-burroughs-john:
John Burroughs, American poet and writer on nature, was born in Roxbury in New York on 3 April 1837 and is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His early years spread across teaching, journalism, farming, and fruit growing. For nine years he worked as a clerk in the treasury department at Washington. A book on Walt Whitman as poet and person came out in 1867.

In 1871 Wake-Robin began a long line of books on birds, flowers, and rural scenes. Those books made him the heir of Thoreau as a famed essayist on the life around human homes. Later books took a more thoughtful turn, with more turn to books and musing. The core theme and method stayed the same all the same. Birds and Poets, Locusts and Wild Honey, and Signs and Seasons lead the list.
britannica-1911-byng-john:
John Byng, a British admiral who lived from 1704 to 1757, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the fourth son of George Byng, Lord Torrington, and he entered the navy in 1718. His father's great influence accounts, the entry says, for his rapid rise in the service.

Byng became a lieutenant in 1723 and a captain in 1727. His career shows nothing of note till he was made rear admiral in 1745 and vice admiral in 1747. He served on the most comfortable stations and avoided the harder work of the navy. When the Seven Years War neared, Minorca was threatened from Toulon and was invaded in 1756. Byng, then an admiral in the Channel, was ordered to the Mediterranean to relieve the garrison of Fort Saint Philip. His squadron was not well manned, and his letters show he left prepared for failure.
britannica-1911-byron-hon-john:
John Byron, a British vice admiral who lived from 1723 to 1786, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the second son of the fourth Lord Byron and grandfather of the poet. As a young man he sailed with Anson on his voyage round the world. Hard service and foul storms dogged his many voyages.

Sailors nicknamed him Foul Weather Jack for his luck with gales. In 1760 he led a squadron to Louisburg to wreck its forts. In 1764 he took the Dolphin on a long cruise in the South Seas. His tale of his early adventures came out in 1768, and his grandson drew on it for Don Juan. Byron became governor of Newfoundland in 1769. He rose to vice admiral in 1778 and fought an drawn battle off Grenada the next year.
britannica-1911-cabot-john:
John Cabot (1450-1498), an Italian sailor who found North America for Europe, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Genoa, he went to live in Venice in 1461 and became a citizen there in 1476. On a trade voyage to the east he visited Mecca, then the great mart where goods of the East changed hands for goods of the West.

The article says he asked where the spices, silks, and gems at Mecca came from. He learned they came by caravan from far parts of Asia in the north-east. Knowing the earth is a sphere, he saw that a westward sea route to Asia might be shorter. About 1484 he moved with his family to London. His plans in time reached the chief merchants of Bristol, a port that already traded with Iceland.
britannica-1911-cade-john:
John Cade, commonly called Jack Cade, the English rebel who led the rising of 1450, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He died in 1450 and was probably an Irishman by birth. Little is known of his early life. He seems to have lived in Sussex, fled the country after a murder, and served in the French wars. He returned and settled in Kent under the name Aylmer.

When the men of Kent rose in May 1450, their leader, generally taken to be Cade, led them from Blackheath into London on July 3. Part of the crowd favoured them, but plunder turned opinion against them. After securing the execution of Lord Say and of the sheriff of Kent, the rebels withdrew. On July 5 the citizens kept them out after a fierce fight on London Bridge.
britannica-1911-cairns-john:
John Cairns (1818-1892) was a Scottish Presbyterian divine born in Berwickshire. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows him from herd boy work to top student rank. He kept up schooling while herding and entered Edinburgh in 1834. First place in classics and philosophy marked his degree in 1841.

Berlin study of German thought filled two years before his ordination. He then served one church at Berwick for more than thirty years. Calls to other posts came often, yet he chose to stay put. In 1876 he took a theology chair and later led the college. He learned many tongues to read new work in its own words.
britannica-1911-caius-john:
John Caius, the doctor who refounded a Cambridge college, holds a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Norwich in 1510, he studied first at Gonville Hall, Cambridge. He took his first degree in 1533 and went to Italy. At Padua he learned from Montanus and Vesalius and took his physic degree in 1541. Back in London he joined the College of Physicians.

Caius served as doctor to Edward the Sixth, Mary, and Elizabeth. In 1557 he made his old hall far larger and far richer. He changed its name to Gonville and Caius College and added a new court. He led the college as master from 1559 till near his death in 1573.
britannica-1911-cameron-john:
John Cameron, a Scots church scholar, gets a life of schools and posts in the 1911 Britannica. Born at Glasgow near fifteen seventy nine, he learned in his home town. He taught Greek there for a year, then moved to Bordeaux in France. Chairs in wise thought and in church lore came to him in French schools. At Saumur he held the top post for French Protestants in his field.

Civil strife in France drove him to England in sixteen twenty. The king made him head of Glasgow college two years later. His bent for a bishop led rule and his views on meek rule made him unliked there. He quit in less than a year and went back to France. He died at Montauban at age forty six.
britannica-1911-canning-charles-john:
Charles John Canning, Earl Canning, an English statesman who lived from 1812 to 1862, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was governor general of India during the Mutiny of 1857. The youngest child of George Canning, he was born at Brompton, near London. He was schooled at Christ Church, Oxford, and took first class honours in classics in 1833.

In 1836 Canning entered Parliament for Warwick as a Conservative. On his mother's death in 1837 he took her peerage and sat in the Lords as Viscount Canning. Under Peel he served as under secretary for foreign affairs from 1841. In 1853 he became postmaster general, where he showed great capacity for work and zeal to improve the service. In 1855 the death of Lord Dalhousie opened his Indian post.
britannica-1911-capgrave-john:
Capgrave, John is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an English chronicler and writer of saints' lives. Born at Lynn in Norfolk on the twenty-first of April 1393, he spent most of his life at the order's house there. He became a priest, took a doctorate at Oxford, and joined the Augustinian hermits. He died on the twelfth of August 1464.

The article sorts his large output. Most of his works are theological: sermons, commentaries and lives of saints. His fame as a hagiologist rests on the Nova legenda Angliae, though it reworks an earlier collection. His Chronicle of England, written in English, runs from the Creation to 1417 and was left unfinished. Its section on Henry the Sixth is a contemporary record, if a flattering one.
britannica-1911-cartwright-john:
John Cartwright (1740–1824) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an English parliamentary reformer. He was born at Marnham in Nottinghamshire. His younger brother was Edmund Cartwright, inventor of the power loom. John entered the navy at eighteen. He was present at the capture of Cherbourg. He also served under Hawke against Conflans. On the Newfoundland station he acted as chief magistrate for five years.

When the dispute with the American colonies began, Cartwright held that the colonists had right on their side. He refused a post that promised sure promotion. He would not fight against a cause he thought just. In 1774 he published his first plea for the colonists. Its title was American Independence the Glory and Interest of Great Britain. The entry presents a naval officer who gave up advancement for a political conviction.
britannica-1911-cartwright-sir-richard-j:
Sir Richard John Cartwright (1835– ) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a Canadian statesman born in Kingston, Canada, the son of an army chaplain. He entered the Canadian parliament in 1863 as a Conservative. After federation in 1867 he broke with his party over its financial policy, which he judged extravagant, and by 1870 the breach was complete.

In 1873 Cartwright became finance minister in Alexander Mackenzie's Liberal ministry, where his honesty and economy were beyond doubt, though his economy sometimes ran to extremes. He spent the years from 1878 to 1896 as the Liberals' chief financial critic in opposition. Under Laurier from 1896 he served as minister of trade and commerce, and he represented Canada on the Anglo American joint high commission in 1898 and 1899. Failing health moved him to the senate in 1904.
britannica-1911-carver-john:
John Carver (1575?–1621) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on one of the “Pilgrim Fathers” and the first governor of the Plymouth colony in America. He was probably born in Nottinghamshire about 1575. Religious persecution drove him to Holland about 1607, and he became a deacon in the church at Leiden where John Robinson was pastor. In 1620 he sailed to America in the Mayflower.

Carver had probably been elected governor before the ship left England. After the signing of the famous “Compact,” that election was confirmed, and he was chosen again on 23 March 1621 for the year ahead. Early in April he died, the entry says, from the effects of sunstroke. His governorship thus lasted only months, but the entry fixes his place at the head of the new colony at its founding moment. The account is short and keeps to the few facts the record gives.
britannica-1911-case-john:
John Case (d. 1600) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an English Aristotelian scholar and physician born at Woodstock. He was educated at Oxford and elected to a fellowship at St John's College. His Roman Catholic sympathies forced him to resign the post. He then opened a philosophical school in Oxford, which drew many students.

Case won a great name as a logician and dialectician. He was also an authority on music and a noted physician. The entry describes him as a man of innocent, meek, and studious life, a pleasant talker and a keen teacher, much loved by his pupils. Most of his works were commentaries on Aristotle, covering the Organon, Ethics, Politics, and Physics under curious titles. They sold widely and were often reprinted. He also wrote The Praise of Musicke, published in 1586 and dedicated to Sir Walter Raleigh.
britannica-1911-chandos-sir-john:
John Chandos was one of the most famed English war chiefs of the fourteen hundreds. He is first found at a siege in the early years of the long war with France, and then at a great battle won by the English. At a second great battle it was he who turned the day and saved the life of the Black Prince.

For such work the king made him a knight of a top order, gave him lands in Normandy, and set him as his deputy in France. He held high posts in the royal house as well. As chief of a great French province held by England, he won fresh victories in France and in Spain over a famed Breton foe. Made a local governor, he was struck down at a bridge fight and died the next day.
britannica-1911-chardin-sir-john:
Sir John Chardin, who lived from 1643 to 1713, is the subject of a short life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Paris and trained as a jeweller by his rich father, he left France in 1665 for Persia and India. A first trip won him the support of Shah Abbas the Second. He went back to Persia in 1671 by a long land route and spent four years in study there.

Chardin then moved to London in 1681, became a knight, and worked for the East India Company. His full book of travels came out at Amsterdam in 1711. The text praises the book for its full and true detail. It notes that Montesquieu, Rousseau, and Gibbon all drew on his work.
britannica-1911-cheke-sir-john:
Sir John Cheke (1514–1557) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an English classical scholar, the son of a Cambridge university officer. He was educated at St John's College, Cambridge, and became a fellow in 1529. There he adopted the principles of the Reformation. In 1540, on Henry VIII's foundation of the regius chairs, he was elected professor of Greek.

Among his pupils were Lord Burghley, who married Cheke's sister, and Roger Ascham, who praised him in The Schoolmaster. With Sir Thomas Smith he brought in a new method of Greek pronunciation. Bishop Gardiner decreed against it in 1542, but Cheke triumphed in the end. In 1544 he was chosen as tutor to Prince Edward. He sat in parliament, was knighted in 1551, and became a secretary of state in 1553.
britannica-1911-clare-john:
Clare, John (1793–1864) was an English poet, commonly known as the Northamptonshire Peasant Poet, son of a farm labourer, born at Helpstone near Peterborough on 13 July 1793. Taken from school at seven to tend sheep and geese, he worked on a farm, as a pot-boy, a gardener at Burghley Park, a militiaman and a lime burner. By 1818 he was obliged to accept parish relief. Thomson's Seasons, bought from scanty earnings, had set him writing poems.

A Stamford bookseller, Drury, found his poem The Setting Sun and brought him to publisher John Taylor, who issued Poems Descriptive of Rural Life and Scenery in 1820. The Village Minstrel followed in 1821 to high praise, and patrons and subscriptions gave him 45 pounds a year. New wants outran that income, and by 1823 he was nearly penniless again. The Shepherd's Calendar of 1827 met with little success, even as he hawked it himself.
britannica-1911-cleveland-john:
Cleveland, John (1613–1658) was an English poet and satirist, born at Loughborough and baptised on 20 June 1613, son of a clergyman. Educated at Hinckley school, he entered Christ's College, Cambridge, at fifteen and won a fellowship at St John's in 1634. His Latinity and oratory won Fuller's warm praise, and he took his master's degree in 1635. He eagerly opposed Cromwell's candidature as member for Cambridge.

When the Puritan party triumphed he went to Oxford in 1643 and was warmly received by the king, whom he followed to Newark. Deprived of his fellowship as a malignant in 1645, he served as judge-advocate in the Newark garrison until its surrender. His poem The Rebel Scot vented his anger at the Scots handing Charles to Parliament. After prison at Yarmouth and release by Cromwell's order, he died at Gray's Inn on 29 April 1658.
britannica-1911-clifford-john:
Clifford, John (1836– ) was a British Nonconformist minister and politician, born on 16 October 1836 at Sawley in Derbyshire, son of a warp-machinist. As a boy he worked in a lace factory, where Baptist leaders noticed him and sent him to be educated for the ministry. Called to Praed Street chapel, Paddington, in 1858, he studied at University College and the British Museum. London degrees followed in a long run, arts, science, law, through 1866.

At Westbourne Park chapel from 1877 he won a large following as preacher, writer, propagandist and ardent Liberal. He presided over the London Baptist Association, the Baptist Union twice and the National Council of Evangelical Churches. Chief political prominence came from 1903, leading passive resistance to the Education Act of 1902. His own goods were distrained rather than pay tax toward denominational teaching, and the movement shared in the Unionist defeat of January 1906.
britannica-1911-climax-john:
Climax, John (c. 525–600 A.D.) was an ascetic and mystic, also called Scholasticus and Sinaïtes, who spent forty years in a cave at the foot of Mount Sinai. After those forty years he became abbot of the monastery there. His life was written by Daniel, a monk of the monastery of Raithu on the Red Sea. The entry thus places a long cave solitude before a late abbacy in its subject's career.

He takes his name Climax, or Climacus, from his work of the same name, the Ladder to Paradise, in thirty sections. Those sections correspond to the thirty years of the life of Christ, a pattern stated plainly here. The book is written in a simple and popular style, despite its mystic subject. Its first part treats of the vices that hinder holiness, and the second of the virtues of a Christian.
britannica-1911-coke-sir-john:
Sir John Coke (1563–1644) was an English politician born on 5 March 1563. He studied at Trinity College, Cambridge. On leaving, he entered public life in the service of William Cecil, Lord Burghley. He became deputy-treasurer of the navy, then a commissioner of the navy. His work on naval business won him warm praise.

He sat for Warwick in 1621 and was knighted in 1624. He later sat for Cambridge university. In the parliament of 1625 he acted as secretary of state. His set appointment dates from September that year. He brought the king's requests for money before the House. He also defended the foreign policy of Charles I and Buckingham. The leaders of the popular party disliked him. Yet Charles prized his hard work in the years without a parliament. He held his post until 1639.
britannica-1911-colet-john:
John Colet, who lived from about 1467 to 1519, was an English churchman and teacher. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica honors his school founding. He was the eldest son of a lord mayor of London. He studied at Oxford and took his master degree in 1490.

Travel in France and Italy gave Colet new learning and Greek. Erasmus and other great scholars became his friends abroad. Back at Oxford he lectured on the letters of Paul. His fresh plain method broke with dry school custom. As dean of Saint Pauls he set up a free lecture series. Rich by his father death, he refounded Saint Pauls School. Lay merchants, not clergy, ran that school as trustees. That choice was a first in English schooling history.
britannica-1911-colville-john:
John Colville, who lived from about 1540 to 1605, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a Scottish churchman and author, son of Robert Colville of Cleish. He studied at St Andrews University and became a Presbyterian minister. In practice, though, his real trade was political intrigue.

The article says Colville sent secret reports on Scottish affairs to the English government. He joined the Earl of Gowrie's party and took part in the Raid of Ruthven in 1582. For a short time he sat on the judicial bench and in parliament. In 1591 he was caught up in the Earl of Bothwell's attack on Holyrood Palace.
