Outlawed for that act, he fled abroad and died at Paris in 1605. His letters from 1582 to 1603 were printed long after his death.
britannica-1911-comyn-john:
Comyn, John is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Scottish baron (died about 1300) of the wars with Edward the First. He fought for Henry the Third at Northampton and Lewes and was held prisoner for a time in London. In 1286 he became one of the guardians of Scotland, and when the Maid of Norway died in 1290 he stood among the claimants to the throne.

Comyn did not press his own claim; like the rest of his house he backed John de Baliol. The article gives as much room to his son John, the Red Comyn, who guarded Scotland after Falkirk in 1298 and led the fight against Edward for five years. His end came at Dumfries in 1306, stabbed in a heated meeting with Robert the Bruce.
britannica-1911-conington-john:
John Conington was an English scholar of Latin who lived in the mid eighteen hundreds. The 1911 Britannica entry notes that he knew his letters as a small child and read well by age three and a half. He went to school at Beverley and Rugby, then to Oxford, where he won prize after prize in classics and verse.

The entry tells how he tried the law in London, found it dull, and gave up a rich prize to go back to Oxford. There he took the first chair of Latin letters at a college that had just set it up. From then on he gave his life to Latin works, save for one verse rendering of the last books of the Iliad, done to keep a pledge to a friend.
britannica-1911-constable-john:
John Constable is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of an English landscape painter. He lived from 1776 to 1837. He was born at East Bergholt in Suffolk. His father held water mills at Dedham and Flatford. He also held two windmills in the area. John, the second son, was set to work at seventeen. That came after he left Dedham grammar school.

From boyhood he was devoted to painting as an art. He studied in spare hours with a local glazier, John Dunthorne. He met Sir George Beaumont, a keen patron of the arts. The sight of a Claude canvas fired his zeal. Drawings by Girtin in that house fired it further. His father let him visit London in 1795. There the painter Joseph Farington saw his gift at once. Farington gave him hints on craft and method. An engraver named Smith also taught him in that time.
britannica-1911-conybeare-william-john:
William John Conybeare, an English divine who lived from 1815 to 1857, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of Dean Conybeare and was born in August 1815. He was schooled at Westminster and at Trinity College in Cambridge, where he was made a fellow in 1837. From 1842 to 1848 he was head of the Liverpool Collegiate Institution.

He left that post for the vicarage of Axminster. He brought out essays on church and social themes in 1856 and a novel on the causes of unbelief. He is best known as joint author, with Howson, of a life and letters of St Paul, printed in 1851. That book set his name in the minds of church readers of the age. He died at Weybridge in 1857, at the age of forty-two.
britannica-1911-coode-sir-john:
Sir John Coode, an English engineer who lived from 1816 to 1892, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Bodmin in Cornwall, the son of a solicitor. After early work in the west of England, he set up a London practice. In 1847 he took charge of the great harbour works then rising at Portland.

Coode became engineer-in-chief at Portland in 1856 and held the post until the works were done in 1872. That service earned him a knighthood. The article calls him the leading voice of his day on harbour building. Colonial governments in South Africa and Australia sought his advice, as did the government of India. His best known later work was the harbour of Colombo in Ceylon.
britannica-1911-cosin-john:
John Cosin, an English divine who lived from 1594 to 1672, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Norwich and schooled there and at Caius College in Cambridge. On taking orders he served as secretary to one bishop and as chaplain to Bishop Neile of Durham. In 1624 he gained a post at Durham.

Cosin first won note as an author in 1627 with a book of private prayers. It was made, the title said, at the command of Charles the First for the queen's maids of honour. His stress on ritual and his friendship with Laud drew Puritan attack. Prynne and Burton hit at the book hard. In 1634 he became master of Peterhouse, and in 1640 vice-chancellor and dean of Peterborough. The Long Parliament soon took up charges against him.
britannica-1911-craig-john:
John Craig, a Scots reformer born about 1512 who died in 1600, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of Craig of Craigston, who was killed at Flodden in 1513. Craig studied at Saint Andrews and taught the sons of an English border lord. He joined the Dominican order, but soon fell under charge of heresy.

In Italy, with help from Cardinal Pole, he rose to train new friars at Bologna. Reading the Institutes of Calvin revived his doubts, and he was condemned to be burnt. A riot on the death of Pope Paul the Fourth in 1559 broke open his prison and freed him. He preached at Vienna under guard of the archduke, then came home in 1560. In 1562 he became a fellow minister with Knox in Edinburgh, and he clashed with nobles over church lands and rights.
britannica-1911-crawfurd-john:
John Crawfurd (1783–1868), a Scottish orientalist, was born on Islay on 13 August 1783. After study at Edinburgh he became a surgeon in the East India Company service. He served in Java during the British occupation of 1811 to 1817, where his local knowledge proved of great use. In 1821 he was envoy to Siam and Cochin-China, and in 1823 he became governor of Singapore. A hard mission to Burma in 1827 was his last post in the East.

Back in England, Crawfurd was elected president of the Ethnological Society in 1861, and he died at South Kensington on 11 May 1868. His History of the Indian Archipelago appeared in 1820, and he published journals of his embassies to Ava, Siam, and Cochin-China. He also wrote on tax in India and against the duty on paper and newspapers. His Malay grammar and dictionary of 1852 closed the list the entry gives.
britannica-1911-crome-john:
John Crome (1769–1821) was an English landscape painter, founder and chief figure of the Norwich School. He was born at Norwich on 21 December 1769, the son of a weaver, and is often called Old Crome to set him apart from his son. A scant education and humble work led him to a house-painter's apprenticeship. There he painted signboards and sketched from nature. A rich friend's help let him become a drawing-master instead.

Crome studied a collection of Dutch pictures and gained further help from Sir William Beechey in London. In 1805 the Norwich Society of Artists took shape, with Crome as president and largest contributor. His pupils included James Stark and John Thirtle, and J. S. Cotman worked in his circle. His subjects came almost wholly from his native county, and fidelity to nature was his ruling aim. He died at Norwich on 22 April 1821, and his etchings appeared in 1834.
britannica-1911-crowne-john:
John Crowne, a British dramatist who died about 1703, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He was a native of Nova Scotia, where his father had gained a grant of land from Cromwell. The French seized that property, and the home government did nothing to uphold his rights. When the son came to England, poverty shaped his start.

He worked as a gentleman usher to a lady of quality, the entry says. He began his writing career with a romance in 1665, on a coy lady of Thessaly. A romantic play followed in 1671, with no claim to be a true history. The earl of Rochester then won him a court commission for a masque. That move was meant, it seems, to vex Dryden by cutting into his rights as poet laureate.
britannica-1911-cuza-alexander-john:
Alexander John Cuza, first prince of Rumania, born in eighteen twenty, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Galatz in Moldavia, he came of an old noble house of that land. He was schooled at more than one town of high study in the west and in Greece. Past a brief span in arms he went to Paris for more study.

In eighteen forty five he wed the daughter of a peer house. That wife in time set up a home for lone young folk at the chief town. Cuza was jailed by the Russian power for his part in the rising of eighteen forty eight. He fled that jail to Vienna in the end. On his home come in eighteen fifty he was made the head of his home town.
britannica-1911-dee-john:
Dee, John is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an English mathematician and astrologer. He was born in London on the thirteenth of July 1527 and died in 1608. His father was, by one account, a wealthy wine merchant. In 1542 he was sent to Saint John's College, Cambridge.

After five years of work on mathematics and the stars, he went to Holland to visit leading men of those studies. He came home after near a year and was elected a fellow of the new Trinity College. He took his master's degree in 1548. That same year he had to leave England. Men suspected him of conjuring, a charge first roused by a stage machine of his. It showed a beetle flying up to Jupiter with a man and a basket of food on its back.
britannica-1911-demijohn:
A demijohn is a glass bottle or jar with a large round body and a narrow neck, cased in wicker-work and fitted with handles. The word also serves for an earthenware jar covered the same way. Sizes run from two to twelve gallons, and the common size holds five gallons, so the vessel serves for storing and carrying liquids in bulk.

The entry traces the name, following the New English Dictionary, to the French Dame Jeanne, or Dame Jane. Giving a personal name to a thing is a common habit, the entry notes, pointing to Toby for a kind of jug and the many uses of Jack. The wicker case guards the glass and gives the carrier his grip.
britannica-1911-elias-john:
John Elias, who lived from 1774 to 1841, was a Welsh preacher and reformer. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his birth in Carnarvonshire. The Calvinistic Methodist revival caught him young, and he preached at nineteen. In 1799 he settled in Anglesey, trading weaving for a small shop. Under Thomas Charles of Bala he founded many Sunday schools. He also won Welsh support for mission and Bible societies.

When Charles died in 1814, Elias led the Calvinistic Methodist church. His life from then is a record of preaching tours. Ten thousand people came to his funeral in 1841. Men called him the Welsh Demosthenes for his power in the pulpit. His strength lay in conviction and in dramatic presentation. He helped frame his church's Confession of Faith in 1823. In politics he was a firm Tory and opposed Catholic emancipation.
britannica-1911-eliot-john:
John Eliot is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was a clergyman in colonial America from 1604 to 1690. He was known as the Apostle to the Indians. He was baptized in Hertfordshire in August 1604. His father was a farmer of the middle class. He took a degree at Cambridge in the year 1622.

He worked as a helper in a school run by Thomas Hooker. That link turned him toward the Puritan way of faith. In 1631 he sailed for America to flee curbs on his faith. He settled first at Boston and then at Roxbury. He served the church at Roxbury till his death. He wed a woman who had been pledged to him in England. A drive to convert the Indians then shaped his life. He learned their tongues with the help of a young Indian.
britannica-1911-eliot-sir-john:
Sir John Eliot (1592-1632), an English statesman, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Port Eliot in Cornwall, the seat of an old Devonshire family lately settled there. He entered Exeter College at Oxford in 1607 and left after three years to study law. He also spent some months travelling in France, Spain, and Italy, in part with the young George Villiers.

The article says he entered Parliament at just twenty-two, as member for St Germans in the parliament of 1614. Knighted in 1618, he gained through Villiers the post of vice-admiral of Devon, with wide powers over the defence and trade of the county. His energy in the post soon brought him trouble. In 1623 he trapped the noted pirate John Nutt, who had harried the southern coast for years.
britannica-1911-elliotson-john:
Elliotson, John (1791–1868), was an English physician born at Southwark, London, on 29 October 1791. He studied medicine at Edinburgh and then at Cambridge, taking the degree of M.D. at both. In 1831 he became professor of the principles and practice of physic in London University. In 1834 he became physician to University College hospital.

Elliotson studied phrenology and mesmerism, and his work in mesmerism brought him into conflict with the hospital's medical committee. In December 1838 he resigned his posts at the hospital and the university over that clash. He kept up the practice of mesmerism, held séances at home, edited a magazine called The Zoist, and founded a mesmeric hospital in 1849. The entry also credits him as an early teacher of clinical lecturing and an early backer of the stethoscope. He died in London on 29 July 1868.
britannica-1911-ericsson-john:
Ericsson, John (1803–1889), was a Swedish-American naval engineer born at Langbanshyttan in Wermland, Sweden, on 31 July 1803. He was the second son of Olaf Ericsson, an inspector of mines. Showing a strong bent for mechanics from his earliest years, he was at work at twelve as a draughtsman for the Swedish Canal Company. From 1820 to 1827 he served in the army and rose to captain.

In 1826 Ericsson went to London, and with John Braithwaite he built the “Novelty,” a locomotive entered for the Rainhill trials of 1829, where Stephenson's “Rocket” took the prize. He planned marine engines set wholly below the water-line, made for Captain Ross's Arctic voyage of 1829, though they did not prove satisfactory. In 1833 his caloric engine was made public. In 1836 he took out a patent for a screw-propeller, and the entry takes up the fight over who was first with that device.
britannica-1911-fastolf-sir-john:
Sir John Fastolf, who died in 1459, was an English soldier whose name lived on in part as a model for Shakespeare's Falstaff. Son of a Norfolk gentleman, he is said to have served as squire to Thomas Mowbray, duke of Norfolk, before 1398. He campaigned in Ireland in 1405 and 1406, married a wealthy widow in 1408, and served in Gascony in 1413.

Fastolf fought through Henry V's later campaigns in France and became governor of Maine and Anjou in 1423. He won the so-called battle of herrings in 1429, yet defeat at Patay that year brought charges of cowardice. His Garter was taken away, then restored after inquiry. He served until 1440, held estates in Norfolk, Suffolk and Southwark, and died at Caister on 5 November 1459.
britannica-1911-fawcett-john:
John Fawcett (1768-1837), English actor and playwright, was born on 29 August 1768, son of an actor of the same name who died in 1793. At eighteen he ran away from school and appeared at Margate as Courtall in The Belle's Stratagem. He then joined Tate Wilkinson's company and turned from tragedy to low comedy parts, the line in which his talent lay.

Fawcett reached Covent Garden in 1791 and the Haymarket in 1794. Colman, manager of the Haymarket, wrote parts designed to suit him. Two of his greatest successes were Dr Pangloss in The Heir at Law in 1797 and Dr Ollapod in The Poor Gentleman in 1798. The entry is short, giving his family, his start, and his chief roles. He retired from the stage in 1830, seven years before his death.
britannica-1911-feckenham-john:
John Feckenham (about 1515-1584), English churchman and last abbot of Westminster, was born at Feckenham in Worcestershire to a yeoman family named Howman. He took his territorial name on entering religion. Taught first by the parish priest, he went to the cloister school at Evesham and then to Gloucester Hall, Oxford, as a Benedictine student. Professed at Evesham, he took his B.D. in 1539, months before the abbey was surrendered to the king in January 1540.

Feckenham served as chaplain to Bishop Bell and then to Bonner, gaining fame as a preacher and a disputant of keen mind and steady charity. Cranmer sent him to the Tower about 1549, yet he was borrowed out of prison for seven public disputations. Queen Mary freed him in 1553 and restored him to favour. After long suffering for his conscience under Elizabeth, he died in prison and was buried at Wisbech on 16 October 1584.
britannica-1911-felton-john:
John Felton, born about 1595 and dead in 1628, was the man who killed the duke of Buckingham. The 1911 Britannica entry draws him as a soldier whose career went wrong from the start. He came from an old Suffolk family and served as a lieutenant at Cadiz in 1625. A wound left his left hand weak, and a grim temper made him few friends.

Each bid for promotion was refused, and even his scant pay from Cadiz went unpaid. Buckingham told him to his face that he might hang when he begged a captain post. Want, insult, and printed attacks on the duke fed his hate. The entry shows the slow build of grievance that led to the killing.
britannica-1911-fernandez-john:
John Fernandez, a Portuguese traveller of the fourteen hundreds, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He may have been the earliest modern explorer of the uplands of West Africa. The article also calls him a pioneer of the Guinea trade in slaves and gold. He first appears as a captive of the Barbary Moors, before 1445.

Among his captors Fernandez learned Arabic and formed a plan of inland travel. In 1445 he offered to stay in Guinea and gather facts for Prince Henry the Navigator. He landed at the River of Gold and went inland with native shepherds. He stayed seven months in that country, just within Muslim Africa. His report covered the land, its climate, its beasts and plants in rich detail. It also covered the peoples there, their tongues, faith, roving habits, and trade. He sailed on later voyages in 1446 and 1447.
britannica-1911-fitch-john:
John Fitch was an American first maker of steam sail craft who lived from seventeen forty-three to seventeen ninety-eight. He was born at Windsor, the son of a farm man. He went to sea young, then worked as a clock man, a brass man, and a plate man. War work as a food man to the troops won him funds.

He bought land, mapped the west wilds, and there got the thought of steam on great streams. Cash was hard to raise, and law houses gave praise but no funds. A firm at last built his boat, which took fares on the Delaware in seventeen ninety. Loss broke the firm.
britannica-1911-flamsteed-john:
John Flamsteed (1646-1719), English astronomer, was born at Denby near Derby on 19 August 1646, the only son of a maltster. Rheumatic joints, caught from a chill while bathing, ended his schooling at Derby in May 1662. Failed cures, even a trip to Ireland in 1665 to be stroked by Valentine Greatrakes, left him to study astronomy alone. He read Sacrobosco, watched a partial eclipse in 1662, and tried building measuring tools.

A tract on the equation of time, printed by Wallis in 1673, and a paper in the Philosophical Transactions won him wide notice by 1670. He met Newton at Cambridge and took an M.A. by letters patent. The entry follows him to Greenwich, where his observations built the first Greenwich star catalogue. His great work, Historia coelestis Britannica, appeared in three folio volumes in 1725, after his death, gathering a lifetime of exact watching of the skies.
britannica-1911-flavel-john:
John Flavel (about 1627-1691), English Presbyterian divine, was born at Bromsgrove in Worcestershire, probably in 1627. His father Richard was described in the records of the time as a painful and eminent minister. Educated at home, at grammar schools and at University College, Oxford, Flavel took orders in 1650. He held a curacy at Diptford in Devon, succeeded its vicar, and moved in 1656 to Dartmouth, the town tied to his name.

The Act of Uniformity ejected Flavel from his living in 1662, yet he kept preaching in private until the Five Mile Act drove him to Slapton in 1665. After a spell in London he returned to Dartmouth and worked there until his death in 1691. He married four times. A vigorous and copious writer, he left works such as Navigation Spiritualized, The Fountain of Life in forty-two sermons, The Method of Grace and a treatise on the soul of man.
britannica-1911-flaxman-john:
John Flaxman (1755-1826), English sculptor and draughtsman, was born at York on 6 July 1755 during a short stay by his parents. His father kept a respected trade as a moulder and seller of plaster casts at Covent Garden in London. The family returned to London within six months. Flaxman spent a sickly childhood in his father's back shop, high-shouldered and weakly, with a head large for his body. His mother died when he was about ten.

Regular schooling was thin, and Flaxman picked up most of his education himself. The long entry follows him from the cast shop to fame. It traces his sculpture, his drawings and the monuments that made his name. A frail boy from a tradesman's workshop rose to the front rank of English art. The opening pages also tell of his stepmother and of a forefather said to have fought for parliament at Naseby.
britannica-1911-floyer-sir-john:
Sir John Floyer (1649-1734), English physician and author, was born at Hinters in Staffordshire and educated at Oxford. He practised medicine at Lichfield. It was by his advice that Dr Johnson, as a child, was taken by his mother to London. There the boy was touched by Queen Anne for the king's evil on 30 March 1714. Floyer died on 1 February 1734, after a long life in practice.

Floyer championed cold bathing, brought in the practice of counting the pulse rate, and gave an early account of the lung changes found with emphysema. His writings include a Touchstone of Medicines of 1687, judging plants, minerals and animals by taste and smell. He also wrote on animal humours and on the right use of baths. A treatise on asthma and an essay on cold bathing followed.
britannica-1911-forbes-sir-john:
Sir John Forbes (1787-1861), British physician, was born at Cuttlebrae in Banffshire in 1787. He went to grammar school at Aberdeen and then to Marischal College. After nine years as a surgeon in the navy he took his M.D. at Edinburgh in 1817. He began practice at Penzance, moved to Chichester in 1822, and settled in London in 1840. The next year he was appointed physician to the royal household, and in 1853 he was knighted for his services.

Forbes was better known as an author and editor than as a practical physician, the entry says plainly. His works include case studies of 1824 illustrating the stethoscope and percussion in diseases of the chest. He wrote on modern mesmerism in 1845 and A Physician's Holiday in 1849. His memorandums made in Ireland in the autumn of 1852 also appear in the list. He died at Whitchurch in Berkshire on 13 November 1861.
britannica-1911-ford-john:
John Ford (1586-about 1640), English dramatist, was baptized on 17 April 1586 at Ilsington in north Devon. He came of a good family: his father sat in the commission of the peace, and his mother was a sister of Sir John Popham, attorney-general and lord chief justice. Ford matriculated at Exeter College, Oxford, in 1601. Like a cousin of the same name, he turned to the law and entered the Middle Temple in 1602, though he seems never to have been called to the bar.

Four years later Ford made his first appearance as an author with an elegy, Fame's Memorial, on the dead earl of Devonshire. The long entry traces his plays one by one: The Lover's Melancholy, The Broken Heart, Perkin Warbeck and 'Tis Pity She's a Whore. Editions by Gifford and Dyce close the account.
britannica-1911-foster-john:
John Foster (1770-1843), English author and dissenting minister, was generally known as the Essayist. He was born in a small farmhouse near Halifax in Yorkshire on 17 September 1770. His parents were grave and severe, and he lacked proper companions. His early years were wrapped in a gloomy, sombre air that never wholly left him. His youthful energy, finding no outlet, turned inward into a morbid intensity of thought and feeling, by his own account present before he was twelve.

Foster's parents added weaving to their small farm income, and the boy helped by spinning wool. The entry follows him from that farmhouse to the Baptist ministry and to fame as a writer. His essays, above all those on popular literature and on the evils of popularity, made his name. Readers get the portrait of a shy, intense thinker whose solitude shaped a brooding prose style.
britannica-1911-fowler-john:
John Fowler (1826-1864), English inventor, was born at Melksham in Wiltshire on 11 July 1826. He learned practical engineering at Middlesbrough-on-Tees. About 1850 he invented a mechanical system for the drainage of land, the mole drain work by which his name first spread. In 1852 he began experiments in steam cultivation, ploughing by engine and cable instead of by horse. In 1858 the Royal Agricultural Society gave him a prize of 500 pounds. The prize was for a steam-cultivator fit to replace plough or spade.

In 1860 Fowler founded at Hunslet, Leeds, the firm of Fowler and Co., makers of agricultural machinery, traction engines and the like. The firm carried his system across the farms of Britain and far beyond. He died at Ackworth in Yorkshire on 4 December 1864, only thirty-eight years old. His short entry stands in a shared file with the life of Sir John Fowler.
britannica-1911-fowler-sir-john:
Sir John Fowler (1817-1898), English civil engineer, was born on 15 July 1817 at Wadsley Hall near Sheffield, where his father was a land-surveyor. At sixteen he became a pupil of John Towlerton Leather, engineer of the Sheffield water-works. Leather's uncle George was engineer of the Aire and Calder Navigation and the Goole Docks. Fowler worked for both men at times and gained a thorough grounding in hydraulic engineering, the art of docks, rivers and water supply, before the railway age swept him up.

Railway work soon claimed Fowler and his employers. One of his first jobs was to oppose the Midland railway route chosen by the Stephensons, which left Sheffield on a branch line. The Stephensons' prestige carried the day in that fight. The long entry follows Fowler into his great works for the railways of Britain and Egypt. His name stood with the Metropolitan Railway and the Forth Bridge.
britannica-1911-foxe-john:
John Foxe (1516-1587) was the author of the famous Book of Martyrs. He was born at Boston in Lincolnshire in 1516. At sixteen he is said to have entered Brasenose College, Oxford, as pupil of John Harding. His room-mate was Alexander Nowell, afterwards dean of St Paul's. His firm university link, though, is with Magdalen College. He took his B.A. in 1537 and his M.A. in 1543, lectured on logic in 1540-1541, and became a fellow of Magdalen in 1539, resigning in 1545.

Foxe wrote several Latin plays on scriptural subjects. The best, De Christo triumphante, was printed repeatedly and translated by Richard Day. It is said he refused the rules for regular chapel attendance and protested against them. The long entry follows the fellow turned exile and martyrologist. His Book of Martyrs, the Acts and Monuments, fixed the memory of the Marian burnings in the English mind for centuries after his death.
britannica-1911-franklin-sir-john:
Sir John Franklin (1786-1847), English rear-admiral and Arctic explorer, was born at Spilsby in Lincolnshire on 16 April 1786. Destined at first for the church, he chose the sea, fought at Copenhagen in 1801 as a midshipman, and learned surveying under his cousin Matthew Flinders on the coasts of Australia. He later served at Trafalgar and in the New Orleans campaign.

From 1819 Franklin led an overland party from Hudson Bay to the Arctic Sea, charting the coast east of the Coppermine river. The return across the Barren Ground brought terrible suffering. The entry follows his later Arctic work and lost final voyage, the relics brought home by search parties, and the searches by Hall and Schwatka that added nothing new. A monument in Westminster Abbey marks his fame, and Lady Franklin kept his name before the public until her death in 1875.
britannica-1911-galt-john:
John Galt (1779-1839) was a Scottish novelist, born at Irvine in Ayrshire on 2 May 1779. The 1911 Britannica entry follows him from clerk's work and wide reading to London in 1804, travel for merchants testing Napoleon's trade decrees, and meetings with Byron at Gibraltar, Malta and Athens. His early books were lives, travels and histories; fiction came later.

His name rests on humorous studies of Scottish life: The Ayrshire Legatees, The Annals of the Parish, The Provost, The Entail and Lawrie Todd. The entry singles out the Annals, told by the Rev. Micah Balwhidder, as a true picture of a country parish. In 1826 Galt went to Canada as secretary of the Canada Land Company, founded Guelph, and came home ruined in 1829 to write until his death.
britannica-1911-gau-john:
John Gau (about 1495 to about 1553) was a Scottish translator, born at Perth and educated at St Salvator's College, St Andrews. The 1911 Britannica entry places him at Malmo in 1533, perhaps as chaplain to the Scots community there. That year the exiled Antwerp printer John Hochstraten issued his book, The Richt vay to the Kingdome of Heuine.

The entry calls it the first Scottish book written on the Reformers' side. It is a translation of Christiern Pedersen's Danish work of 1531, with signs of use of a German version too. Only one copy survives, at Britwell Court; the rest may have been seized at sea as heretical cargo, the entry suggests. Gau married a Malmo citizen's daughter, Birgitta, in 1536. She died in 1551, and he died in or about 1553.
britannica-1911-gerard-john:
John Gerard, an English herbalist and surgeon who lived from 1545 to 1612, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Nantwich in Cheshire toward the end of 1545, he was schooled near his home town and, after some time in travel, settled in London to practise his craft. For more than twenty years he also ran the London and Theobalds gardens of Lord Burghley.

In 1596 Gerard published a catalogue of the plants grown in his own Holborn garden, more than a thousand kinds in all, with both English and Latin names. His famed Herball followed in 1597. He called it the first fruits of his own labours, but the entry shows it rests on a translation of Dodoens, arranged by Lobel. Of its many pictures, only sixteen seem to be new, the rest being printed from wood blocks used at Frankfurt in 1590.
britannica-1911-gerard-knight-of-st-john: Gerard is a short life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the founder of the order of the knights of Saint John of Jerusalem. Born near the year ten forty, he came to Jerusalem as a soldier or a trader. There he took charge of a rest house for pilgrims who came to see the holy places. He shaped that house into a formal order, which won papal backing in the year eleven thirteen. He died in the year eleven twenty.
britannica-1911-gerson-john:
John Gerson lived from 1363 to 1429 and was a French scholar and divine. The 1911 Britannica life gives his full name as Jean Charlier de Gerson. He was chancellor of the university of Paris in his prime. He was the ruling spirit at the councils of Pisa and Constance. He was born at the village of Gerson in December 1363.

His parents were devout peasants with twelve children in all. Seven of those twelve gave their lives to the church in vows. At age fourteen young Gerson was sent to the college of Navarre. After five years he took the licentiate of arts at Paris. He then read theology under Gilles des Champs and Pierre d'Ailly.
britannica-1911-gibson-john:
Gibson, John, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of an English sculptor. Born near Conway in 1790, he was the son of a market gardener. His mother is said to have given him his drive and grit. At age nine the family set out for America but stopped at Liverpool.

There the print shop windows seized the boy's eye and mind. Too poor to buy prints, he learned to hold each line in memory. He would draw the scene from recall when he got home. In time he could copy whole famed works this way from memory. At age fourteen he was placed with a firm of cabinet makers. The work sickened him, and he quit it after a year.
britannica-1911-gilbert-john:
John Gilbert (1810-1889) was an American actor, whose real name was Gibbs. The 1911 Britannica entry is brief: he was born in Boston, Massachusetts, on 27 February 1810, and first appeared there as Jaffier in Venice Preserved. He soon found his true vein was comedy, above all in old-men parts.

In London in 1847 he was well received by press and public alike, and played with Macready. From 1861 to 1888 he was the leading actor at Wallack's theatre in New York. He died on 17 June 1889. The entry closes by pointing to William Winter's Life of John Gilbert, published at New York in 1890, for the full record of his career.
britannica-1911-gilbert-sir-john:
Sir John Gilbert (1817-1897) was an English painter and illustrator, born at Blackheath on 21 July 1817. The 1911 Britannica entry stresses how little teaching he had. A clerk's job in a London estate office came first. His only real instruction was brief lessons in colour from George Lance. In 1836 he showed work in public for the first time.

That first showing, at the Society of British Artists, set his pattern: drawings and oils drawn from Shakespeare and Scott. The entry lists early exhibits such as Inez de Castro and Don Quixote giving advice to Sancho Panza of 1841. The long entry follows the flood of drawings and oil paintings that came after, year by year, on the same literary and historical themes.
britannica-1911-gillies-john:
John Gillies, who lived from 1747 to 1836, was a Scots historian and scholar of Greek. The 1911 Britannica entry traces him from birth at Brechin to study at Glasgow. At age twenty he stood in for the professor of Greek for a short time. In 1786 his History of Ancient Greece came out after two years of work.

That book had worth when Greek history study was still young, and it was turned into French and German. It was written from a strong Whig slant and has since been fully replaced. After the death of Robertson he became royal historian for Scotland. His other works are now little read, the entry notes with candour.
britannica-1911-glas-john:
John Glas (1695-1773) was a Scottish divine, born at Auchtermuchty in Fife on 5 October 1695, where his father was minister. The 1911 Britannica entry follows him through St Andrews and Edinburgh to the parish of Tealing in 1719, where his preaching soon drew a large congregation.

A question on the Shorter Catechism set him examining the New Testament basis of the church. By 1725 he had rejected national covenants and formed a separate society of nearly a hundred members. His conclusions were sharp: no national church has New Testament warrant, the magistrate has no function in the church, and true reformation comes by word and spirit, not politics. The treatise stating this, The Testimony of the King of Martyrs, appeared in 1729. Suspended in 1728 and deposed in 1730, he founded the first Glasite church. The entry, signed by Dugald Macfadyen, follows his later years at Dundee and his collected works.
britannica-1911-goodsir-john:
Goodsir, John, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of a Scottish anatomist. Born at Anstruther in Fife on the 20th of March 1814, he came of a line of doctors. He was schooled at St Andrews and in his home town. In 1830 he was placed with a surgeon-dentist at Edinburgh.

There he studied the body's build under Robert Knox as a teacher. In 1835 he joined his father in practice at Anstruther. Three years later he read a paper on the pulps of human teeth. His work on how teeth grow won praise for its full scope. With Edward Forbes he worked on the study of sea life. In 1840 he moved to Edinburgh for good.
britannica-1911-gower-john:
John Gower (d. 1408) was an English poet who died at a great age in 1408. He was most likely born about 1330 and came from a good Kentish family. One claim links him to a John Gower who held the manor of Kentwell, but the article finds strong faults in that claim. There is no proof he lived as a country gentleman. He did hold wealth, though, and owned the manors of Feltwell and Moulton.

A paper of 1382 calls Gower an esquire of Kent, and he was not in holy orders. His tie with Chaucer is well shown. When Chaucer left for Italy in 1378, he named Gower to act for him while he was gone. Chaucer also sent his Troilus and Criseyde to Gower and Strode for review. He called Gower moral and Strode philosophical in that address. Gower's Confessio Amantis also greets Chaucer.
britannica-1911-greaves-john: John Greaves is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry of which the hosted text preserves only the closing passage. Nothing of the entry's account of his life survives here, and nothing is invented to fill the gap. What remains is the tail of a works list. It names two of his books, both dated 1649: Denarius, and the Elementa linguae Persicae. His miscellaneous works, it adds, were published in 1737 by Dr Thomas Birch, with a biographical notice. The entry's authorities are Smith's Vita quorundam eruditorum virorum and Ward's Gresham Professors.
britannica-1911-greenwood-john:
John Greenwood is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of an English Puritan and Separatist. The date and place of his birth are not known. He died in 1593, the heading notes. He entered Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, in 1577. He took his first degree there in 1581. He held strong Puritan views from early on. Those views led him to the most strict form of Separatism.

Greenwood served as chaplain to Lord Rich at Rochford in Essex. He had been ordained deacon and then priest by two bishops. He soon gave up that ordination as wholly unlawful. By 1586 he led the Separatists of London. Many of that group had been jailed since 1567. He was arrested in October 1586. The next May he was sent to the Fleet prison. The entry sets out a life spent at odds with the state church.
britannica-1911-hamilton-john:
John Hamilton (c. 1511–1571) was a Scottish prelate and politician. He was a natural son of the 1st earl of Arran. Early in life he became a monk and abbot of Paisley. Study at Paris preceded his rise in Scotland. His half-brother, the regent Arran, backed him. He became keeper of the privy seal in 1543. Dunkeld's bishopric followed two years later. In 1546 he succeeded Beaton as archbishop of St Andrews.

He worked hard to halt Protestantism's growth. Persecution, though, was not generally his policy. Hamilton's Catechism served his Catholic campaign in print. Protestants imprisoned him in 1563 once they held power. Released, he became an active partisan of Mary, queen of Scots. He baptised the infant James and pronounced Mary's divorce from Bothwell. After Langside he sheltered in Dumbarton Castle. Seized there, he was hanged on 6 April 1571. The charge was complicity in the Darnley and Murray murders.
britannica-1911-hampden-john:
John Hampden (c. 1595–1643) was an English statesman. He was born about 1595 at Great Hampden in Buckinghamshire. His mother was Oliver Cromwell's aunt. His father's early death left him a good estate. Thame grammar school and Magdalen College, Oxford, educated him. The Inner Temple admitted him in 1613. He first sat in Parliament in 1621 for Grampound. Wendover and Buckinghamshire returned him at later stages.

Popular imagination makes him the revolution's central early figure. His resistance to ship-money fixed that fame. Character explains the rest of it. He was massive yet modest, brave yet charitable. He shielded others from the costs of their actions. He let Eliot, then Pym, take the louder roles. His statue stands in St Stephen's Hall. It types the noblest parliamentary opposition. The long narrative ends by demolishing two beloved legends. His dying prayer and a famous portrait both prove forgeries.
britannica-1911-hancock-john:
John Hancock (1737–1793) was an American Revolutionary statesman. He was born at Braintree, Massachusetts, on 23 January 1737. Harvard graduated him in 1754. He entered his uncle Thomas Hancock's mercantile house in Boston. The uncle had adopted him. In 1764 he inherited a large fortune and the business. Boston made him a selectman in 1765. The general court took him the next year.

Customs officers seized his sloop Liberty in 1768. They charged unpaid duties on a cargo of Madeira. The suits against him failed but made him popular. His resentment of British government hardened. He presided over both Massachusetts Provincial Congresses. Gage's Lexington expedition aimed partly at capturing him and Adams. He presided over the Continental Congress from 1775 to 1777. He signed the Declaration of Independence first. Repeated election as governor proved his popularity. He died at Quincy in 1793.
britannica-1911-harington-sir-john:
Sir John Harington (1561-1612) was an English writer, and his court career is told in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Kelston near Bath, he was godson to Queen Elizabeth, his father having served the princess in her years of danger. He studied at Eton and at Christ's College, Cambridge, taking a master's degree.

The entry relates the tale that the queen, vexed by his racy translation from Ariosto, banished him to Kelston until he had translated the whole work. Orlando Furioso in English verse appeared in 1591. He was high sheriff of Somerset in 1592, and in 1596 published his Ajax works, a set the entry calls collectively very absurd.
britannica-1911-harrison-john:
John Harrison lived from 1693 to 1776 and was an English clock maker. The 1911 Britannica life opens at Faulby near Pontefract in Yorkshire. He was the son of a carpenter and learned that trade at first. The family moved to Barrow in Lincolnshire in the year 1700. Young Harrison earned a bit by land measure work on the side.

His true bent lay with machines and with fine craft in wood. In 1715 he made a clock with wheels of wood throughout. That clock rests now in the patent museum at South Kensington. In 1726 he devised his famed gridiron pendulum for clocks. It holds its length through heat and cold, a key gain for time.
britannica-1911-hawkesworth-john:
John Hawkesworth (c. 1715–1773) was an English miscellaneous writer. He was born in London about 1715. He may have clerked for an attorney. He was certainly self-educated. In 1744 he succeeded Johnson compiling parliamentary debates. The Gentleman's Magazine was his platform. With Johnson he started The Adventurer periodical. It ran to 140 numbers, half of them his. Canterbury rewarded his moral writing with an LL.D.

His twelve-volume Swift edition appeared in 1754–1755. A larger one ran to twenty-seven volumes. He adapted Dryden and Southerne for Drury Lane. His oriental tale Almoran and Hamet appeared in 1761. The admiralty commissioned him to edit Cook's first voyage papers. His three-volume Account appeared in 1773. Publishers reportedly paid him £6,000 for it. Critics attacked his South Seas descriptions as inexact. Their severity is said to have hastened his death.
britannica-1911-hawkshaw-sir-john:
Sir John Hawkshaw (1811–1891) was an English engineer born in Yorkshire. Leeds grammar school educated him. Six or seven years of railway and road work preceded his majority. In 1832 he became engineer to a mining association in Venezuela. The climate broke his health within two years. Liverpool docks employed him under Jesse Hartley on his return. The Manchester, Bury and Bolton Canal followed.

In 1845 he became chief engineer to the Manchester & Leeds railway. Its successor, the Lancashire & Yorkshire, kept him for decades. London practice began in 1850 as a consulting engineer. Charing Cross and Cannon Street railways were his work. Their Thames bridges came from him too. The East London railway runs through Brunel's tunnel under his charge. The Severn Tunnel ranks among the century's great undertakings. He died in London on 2 June 1891.
britannica-1911-hawkwood-sir-john:
Sir John Hawkwood (d. 1394) was an English adventurer in Italy. He won great wealth as a condottiere. Tradition makes him a tanner's son from Sibil Hedingham in Essex. He was apprenticed in London, then soldiered in France. Edward III and the Black Prince led that army. The peace of Bretigny in 1360 freed his company. He collected men-at-arms and moved south to Italy.

His White Company fought for Monferrato against Milan in 1362. Pisa, Florence, Perugia and the pope all hired him in turn. Resigning once over a council's interference showed his pride. Florence paid him 130,000 gold florins in 1375 for neutrality. A pension of 1,200 florins a year followed that bargain. In 1377 he massacred Cesena's inhabitants on a cardinal's orders. Disgust at executioner's work changed his allegiance within months. Temple-Leader's Giovanni Acuto tells his full story.
britannica-1911-hayward-sir-john:
Sir John Hayward (c. 1560–1627) was an English historian born near Felixstowe. Pembroke College, Cambridge, gave him degrees through the LL.D. In 1599 he published his Life and Raigne of King Henrie IV. He dedicated it to the earl of Essex. Elizabeth disliked the book and its dedication. She ordered Bacon to search it for treason. Bacon found none, but much felony, he joked. The sentences, he said, were stolen from Tacitus.

Hayward stayed in prison until about 1601 anyway. James I's accession let him court the new king. Pamphlets on succession and union followed in 1603. In 1610 he became a historiographer of James' Chelsea college. His Lives of the Three Norman Kings appeared in 1613. A knighthood came in 1619. His Edward VI was found among his manuscripts. It was first published in 1630, after his death.
britannica-1911-heathcoat-john:
John Heathcoat (1783–1861) was an English inventor born at Duffield. A framesmith's apprenticeship near Loughborough trained him. He improved the warp-loom to make lace-like mitts. Business at Nottingham drew competing inventors' intrusions. He removed to Hathern, then Loughborough. In 1808 he built a machine imitating real pillow-lace exactly. It was the most complex textile apparatus yet existing. He patented the invention in 1809.

Luddites attacked his Loughborough factory in 1816. They destroyed all 55 lace frames. Damages of £10,000 were assessed but never paid him. He rebuilt at once at Tiverton in Devon. Improved machines ran there by water, then steam. Rivals disputed his patent; a trial in 1816 upheld it. Parliament took him in later life for committee work. His business knowledge was highly valued there. He died near Tiverton in 1861.
britannica-1911-hely-hutchinson-john:
John Hely-Hutchinson (1724–1794) was an Irish lawyer and statesman. He was educated at Trinity College, Dublin. The Irish bar called him in 1748. His marriage in 1751 brought him the name Hutchinson. His wife was heiress to her uncle Richard Hutchinson. He entered the Irish Commons for Lanesborough in 1759. After 1761 he represented Cork city instead. He began with the patriotic opposition party.

Lord Townshend called him parliament's most powerful man. William Gerard Hamilton praised his ability and honesty. Yet he was an inveterate place-hunter too. Lord North joked he would ask the Isle of Man as a potato garden. He became secretary of state in 1777. In 1782 he read Portland's message on Irish independence. Grattan's triumph followed that same day. He supported parliamentary reform late in life. He died at Buxton on 4 September 1794. His wife had been created Baroness Donoughmore in 1785.
britannica-1911-henderson-john:
John Henderson (1747–1785) was an English actor of Scottish descent. He was born in London. His stage debut came at Bath on 6 October 1772. He played Hamlet on that first appearance. Success in Shakespeare earned him the nickname Bath Roscius. A London engagement proved hard to obtain. The Haymarket finally took him as Shylock in 1777. Colman profited considerably from that success.

Sheridan then engaged him for Drury Lane for two years. Covent Garden received him when the companies combined. He played Richard III there in 1778. He created original parts in plays by Cumberland and others. His last appearance was as Horatius in 1785. He died on 25 November that year. Westminster Abbey received his burial. Garrick was jealous of him, and mimicry estranged Colman. Gainsborough, Stewart and Romney all painted his portrait. He co-wrote a practical method for reading English poetry.
britannica-1911-heywood-john:
John Heywood (b. 1497) was an English dramatist and epigrammatist, said to be a native of North Mimms, near St Albans. He was a chorister of the Chapel Royal. From 1521 the king's accounts pay him ten marks a year as a player of the virginals. In 1538 he played an interlude with his children before the Princess Mary.

Heywood's wit and music made him a favourite with Henry VIII and with Mary. Sir Thomas More took an interest in him, and his Epigrams are tied to More's seat at Gobions. Under Edward VI he was charged with denying the king's supremacy and recanted in public in 1554. Under Mary he spoke at her coronation and won a manor lease in Yorkshire. When Elizabeth succeeded, he fled to Malines. By 1587 he is spoken of as dead and gone.
britannica-1911-hill-john:
John Hill (c. 1716–1775), styled Sir John Hill from his Swedish honours, was an English author, said to have been born in Peterborough. Apprenticed to an apothecary, he kept a small shop in Westminster and travelled hunting rare herbs. His first publication was a translation of Theophrastus's History of Stones (1746).

Hill then wrote without pause: magazines, a daily letter called The Inspector, novels, plays and science. His scurrilous attacks bred quarrels with Fielding, Smart and Garrick. From 1759 to 1775 he worked on The Vegetable System, 26 folio volumes with 1,600 engravings, for his patron Lord Bute. Sweden gave him the order of Vasa in 1774. He also grew rich as a quack doctor on vegetable medicines.
britannica-1911-hilton-john:
John Hilton (1804–1878) was a British surgeon, born at Castle Hedingham in Essex. He entered Guy's Hospital in 1824, became demonstrator of anatomy in 1828 and surgeon in 1849. In 1867 he was president of the Royal College of Surgeons and gave the Hunterian oration. His lectures on Rest and Pain (1859–1862) became classics.

Hilton was the greatest anatomist of his time, nicknamed Anatomical John. With the artist Joseph Towne he stocked Guy's with a unique collection of models. As an operator he was cautious rather than brilliant, though the method for opening deep abscesses bears his name. Yet he was the first to reduce an obturator hernia by abdominal section. He died at Clapham in 1878.
britannica-1911-holt-sir-john:
Sir John Holt (1642–1710) was lord chief justice of England, born at Thame, Oxfordshire, in 1642. His father, a lawyer of small success, became a serjeant and was knighted for Tory services. John entered Oriel College, Oxford, at sixteen, and is said to have spent a wild youth, even taking purses on the highway. At Gray's Inn from about 1660 he turned to diligent study, and was called to the bar in 1663.

Holt stood out in the state trials of the day for his bold defence of accused men, being an ardent friend of civil and religious liberty. He became recorder of London in 1685–1686 and king's sergeant, with a knighthood. A ruling against the king's claim to martial law in peacetime cost him the recordership. He helped arrange the settlement that called William III to the throne, and under William he became lord chief justice of the King's Bench.
britannica-1911-home-john:
John Home (1722–1808) was a Scottish dramatic poet, born at Leith on the 22nd of September 1722. His father was town-clerk there and distantly kin to the earls of Home. Home graduated at Edinburgh in 1742, studied divinity, and was licensed in 1745. That year he volunteered against the Pretender, was taken at Falkirk in 1746, and escaped from Doune castle. In July 1746 he was presented to the parish of Athelstaneford.

Home's first play, Agis, founded on Plutarch, was finished in 1747 and refused by Garrick for Drury Lane. His Douglas grew from hearing the ballad of Gil Morrice sung. After five years' labour he took it to London, where Garrick refused it too. Edinburgh staged it on the 14th of December 1756 to overwhelming success, against the presbytery's opposition. Home wisely resigned his charge in 1757.
britannica-1911-hoole-john:
John Hoole (1727-1803) was an English translator and playwright from London. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica places him as a clerk at East India House at seventeen. He rose there to chief auditor of Indian accounts in time. His free hours went to Latin and, above all, Italian study.

He rendered Tasso and Ariosto into English verse over many years. Works by Metastasio and an early poem by Tasso followed in turn. His own plays, Cyrus, Timanthes, and Cleonice, won little success on stage. Johnson praised his verse as correct and smooth, the entry notes. Later versions by other hands replaced his Ariosto in time.
britannica-1911-hooper-john:
John Hooper, bishop of Gloucester and Worcester, who died in 1555, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in Somerset late in the prior century and took a degree at Oxford in 1519. His early years as a monk are hard to trace with care. Records name men of his name in more than one house.

Hooper later served in the household of a well placed patron at court. There he read works by Zwingli and notes by Bullinger on the letters of Paul. That reading turned him to the reformed faith. Fear for his lands and for his safety drove him abroad. His voyage was rough, with two spells in jail and three months at sea. He reached Strassburg in war time, wed there, and moved on to Zurich. Bullinger there confirmed his new views.
britannica-1911-hotham-sir-john:
Sir John Hotham (d. 1645) was an English parliamentarian of a Yorkshire family. He fought on the continent in the early Thirty Years' War, was made a baronet in 1622, and sat for Beverley in the five parliaments between 1625 and 1640. He was sheriff of Yorkshire in 1635. In 1639 the king took from him the governorship of Hull, and he joined the parliamentary party, refusing ship-money.

In January 1642 parliament ordered Hotham to seize Hull, with its great store of munitions; his son John carried out the order. Hotham took command and in April 1642 refused to admit Charles I to the town. Later he promised his prisoner Lord Digby that he would give Hull up, yet when Charles came again he refused a second time and drove off the besiegers. His son, active in Yorkshire and Lincolnshire, soon fell out with the other parliamentary leaders.
britannica-1911-howard-john:
John Howard (1726–1790) was an English philanthropist and prison reformer, born at Hackney, probably on the 2nd of September 1726. His childhood passed at Cardington, near Bedford, where his father, a retired merchant, held a small estate. Apprenticed to London grocers, he bought up his indenture when his father died in 1742 and left him property. Travel followed, and weak health made him an invalid.

Nursed through a sharp illness by his landlady, a widow of fifty-three, Howard married her in 1752 out of gratitude; she died within three years. Sailing then for Portugal, he was taken by a French privateer, an early taste of captivity. As sheriff he turned to the prisons, finding men held for months over unpaid gaolers' fees. In 1777 his State of the Prisons in England and Wales laid the evils bare. He toured Europe's prisons for years, and died of camp fever at Kherson in January 1790.
britannica-1911-howe-john:
John Howe (1630–1706) was an English Puritan divine, born on the 17th of May 1630 at Loughborough, Leicestershire, where his father was vicar. He entered Christ's College, Cambridge, as a sizar in 1647 and took his B.A. the next year. There he knew Ralph Cudworth, Henry More and John Smith, and his mind took the Platonic tinge that marks his writings.

Howe moved to Oxford, becoming fellow and chaplain of Magdalen College, and took his M.A. in 1652. Ordained by Charles Herle, he went in 1654 as perpetual curate to Great Torrington in Devon. His preaching there grew into the treatises on The Blessedness of the Righteous, on which his fame rests. The long life follows him through the troubles of the Puritan clergy after the Restoration, and through the works that kept his name among the great nonconformist writers.
britannica-1911-hunter-john:
John Hunter is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was a British surgeon and body scholar of note. He lived from 1728 to 1793 in Britain. He was born in Lanarkshire in February 1728. He was the youngest of ten children in his house. His father died when Hunter was a young teen. He is said to have made poor gains at school.

He loved country sports more than books as a boy. At seventeen he went to Glasgow to aid a kin trade. He then sought a fixed trade for his life path. His brother ran a famed body school in London. Leave was won to help with cutting work there. He reached London in the autumn of 1748. A first trial at cutting an arm went well for him. Hard work and skill raised him fast in that school.
britannica-1911-jebb-john:
John Jebb, an English church man who lived from 1736 to 1786, is the subject of a brief 1911 Britannica article. He was schooled at Cambridge and made a fellow of Peterhouse in 1761. He had placed second in the math honors of his year. He was a man of free judgment in church matters.

Jebb backed the move of 1771 to end forced assent to the Thirty Nine Articles. In his talks on the Greek Testament he is said to have voiced Socinian views. In 1775 he gave up his Suffolk church posts. Two years later he took a medical degree and practiced in London. The note ends with a second John Jebb, a bishop famed for a book on sacred writing.
britannica-1911-john:
John is a name article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about one of the most common male names in Christian lands. The name goes back to the Hebrew Yohanan, Yahweh has been gracious, and Greek Ioannes, passing into Latin as Joannes. Its forms run across Europe: Giovanni in Italian, Juan in Spanish, Jean in French, Johann in German, Ian in Gaelic, and Janos in Hungarian. Its spread owes much to two bearers in the Gospels, John the Baptist and John the Evangelist, the beloved disciple.

The name has been borne by twenty two popes, though their numbers rest on an old counting error, and by many kings, princes, and saints. The head of the article then lays out the order of the life notices that follow: the Apostle and the Baptist, popes, emperors, kings, princes, saints, and church writers.
britannica-1911-jortin-john:
John Jortin, who lived from 1698 to 1770, was an English church writer. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his birth in London. His father was a Protestant who had fled Brittany. At Charterhouse and then Cambridge he won fame as a Greek scholar. Pope used his help on notes for the Homer translation.

He took church orders in 1724 and held a parish in Cambridgeshire. London posts followed: preacher at a chapel, then Boyle lecturer in 1749. In 1762 he became chaplain to the bishop of London. A stall at St Paul's and the Kensington parish came with it. He was made archdeacon of London in 1764. His chief works cover church history and a life of Erasmus. The entry praises his wide learning and sharp mind. It also notes his wit and his cool, lay like tone on church themes.
britannica-1911-kay-john:
John Kay (1742–1826) was a Scottish caricaturist, born near Dalkeith, where his father was a mason. At thirteen he was apprenticed to a barber and served him for six years. He then went to Edinburgh, where in 1771 he gained the freedom of the city by joining the corporation of barber surgeons.

In 1785, encouraged by the favour that met his first trials at etching, he took down his barber's pole and opened a small print shop in Parliament Square. There he thrived, painting miniatures and issuing at short gaps his sketches and caricatures of the local celebrities and oddities who filled Edinburgh society in that age. He died on the 21st of February 1826. His portraits were gathered by Hugh Paton and issued in 1838 as a series of original portraits and caricature etchings, a record held to be without match for its time and place.
britannica-1911-kempe-john:
John Kempe (c. 1380–1454) was an English cardinal, archbishop of Canterbury, and chancellor. He was the son of Thomas Kempe, a gentleman of Ollantigh near Ashford in Kent, and was born about 1380. He was trained at Merton College, Oxford, and practised as a church lawyer. He sat as an assessor at the trial of Oldcastle, and in 1415 became dean of the Court of Arches.

He then passed into royal service and worked in the government of Normandy, in time becoming chancellor of the duchy. Early in 1419 he was elected bishop of Rochester and consecrated at Rouen that December. He moved to Chichester in February 1421 and to London that November. In the minority of Henry VI he held a chief place in the council as a supporter of Henry Beaufort. He followed Beaufort as chancellor in March 1426, and that year he was raised to the archbishopric of York.
britannica-1911-ker-john:
John Ker (1673–1726) was a Scottish spy, born in Ayrshire on the 8th of August 1673. His true name was Crawfurd, and his father was Alexander Crawfurd of Crawfurdland. He married Anna, the younger daughter of Robert Ker of Kersland, whose only son had been killed at Steinkirk in 1692. In 1697, after buying the family estates from his wife's elder sister, he took the name and arms of Ker.

He became a leader among the extreme Covenanters and used his sway to ease his money troubles. He sold his support at one time to the Jacobites, at another to the government, and when he could to both at once. A government licence of 1707, letting him mix with men of known or suspected disloyalty, proves he was by then the government's paid spy. In his Memoirs Ker claims that he ran a ring of other spies besides.
britannica-1911-kidd-john:
John Kidd, who lived from 1775 to 1851, was an English doctor and earth scholar. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica lists his Oxford posts. He was born at Westminster in September 1775. His father was a naval captain, and Oxford gave him his degrees.

Kidd read chemistry at Oxford from 1801 and soon held its chair. He gave free talks on minerals and rocks under the Ashmolean Museum. Great earth scholars of the next age took their first lessons there. His push helped set up a chair of geology at Oxford. He later held the top medical chair and kept the Radcliffe Library. His books cover minerals, earth theory, and nature fitted to man.
britannica-1911-kirk-sir-john:
Sir John Kirk (1832– ) was a British naturalist and administrator, son of the Reverend John Kirk, born at Barry near Arbroath on the 19th of December 1832. After serving on the civil medical staff through the Crimean War, he was named in February 1858 physician and naturalist to David Livingstone's second expedition to Central Africa.

He was at Livingstone's side through most of his travels over the next five years. He was one of the first four white men to see Lake Nyassa, on the 16th of September 1859. At last, broken in health, he was sent home on the 9th of May 1863. The name he won on that expedition led to his appointment in January 1866 as acting surgeon to the political agency at Zanzibar. In 1868 he became assistant political agent, rising to consul general in 1873 and agent in 1880. He retired from that post in 1887.
britannica-1911-kirkby-john:
John Kirkby (d. 1290) was an English churchman and statesman. He entered the public service as a clerk of the chancery under Henry III. Under Edward I he acted as keeper of the great seal during the frequent absences of the chancellor, Robert Burnell, and was called vice chancellor.

In 1282 the king sent him through the counties and boroughs to gather money, and this and his other services were well rewarded. Though not yet ordained priest, he held several rich benefices in the church. In 1283 he was chosen bishop of Rochester, but the archbishop of Canterbury, John Peckham, opposed him, and he did not press his claim. In 1286, two years after he became treasurer, he was elected bishop of Ely. He was then ordained priest and consecrated by Peckham. He died at Ely on the 26th of March 1290, remembered as a benefactor to his see.
britannica-1911-knox-john:
John Knox (c. 1505–1572) was the Scottish reformer and historian at the centre of one of the longest life articles in this part of the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Even his birth year is in doubt: the claims for 1505, 1513 and 1515 are weighed, and Knox himself said little of his early life. He was a son of William Knox, who lived in or near Haddington, was schooled there, and studied under the scholar John Major, first at Glasgow and then at St Andrews.

The article follows his rise as preacher and leader of the Scottish Reformation, and gives close study to his writings, above all his History of the Reformation. Church order takes up much of the later text: the pattern of ministers, elders, readers and superintendents, drawn from the Genevan church order under Calvin and from the German church in London. His letters are used throughout as a main source.
britannica-1911-kyrle-john:
John Kyrle (1637–1724), known as "the Man of Ross," was an English philanthropist, born in the parish of Dymock, Gloucestershire, on the 22nd of May 1637. His father was a barrister, and the family had lived at Ross in Herefordshire. Coming into the property at Ross, he settled there and gave his life to the good of the little town. He worked for the schooling of its children, alms for its poor, and the mending and adorning of the place itself.

Kyrle loved to make peace between neighbours who had quarrelled,. He was open-handed to the poor and spent all he had on good works, and he worked much in the open air beside the labourers on his farm. He died on the 7th of November 1724 and was buried in the chancel of Ross Church. The Kyrle Society, founded in 1877, keeps his name alive in work for working people.
britannica-1911-la-farge-john:
John La Farge (1835–1910) was an American artist, born in New York on the 31st of March 1835, of French parentage. His grandfather, a painter of miniatures, taught him drawing, and he studied law and architecture before entering the atelier of Thomas Couture in Paris. There he gave his care to the old masters at the Louvre. He began with illustrations to the poets. His closeness to the artist William M. Hunt, with whom he worked at Newport, Rhode Island, shaped him strongly.

From 1866 La Farge was for some years unfit for work. When his strength returned he did decorative work for Trinity church, Boston, in 1876, and turned to stained glass. He became president of the Society of Mural Painters. His commissions include windows for New York churches, the "Battle Window" in Memorial Hall at Harvard, panels for the Congressional Library at Washington, and work at the Capitol at St Paul.
britannica-1911-landen-john:
John Landen (1719–1790) was an English mathematician, and a short life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica paints a solitary figure. He was born at Peakirk near Peterborough on the twenty third of January 1719. He died at Milton, in the same county, in January 1790. He lived a very retired life and saw little of society.

When Landen did mix in society, his dogmatic manner made men shun him. In 1762 he became agent to Earl Fitzwilliam, a post he held near to his death. He first won notice as a mathematician by essays in the Ladies’ Diary for 1744. In 1766 he was elected a fellow of the Royal Society. He knew well the works of the mathematicians of his own time. He has been called the English d’Alembert, for the force of his analysis.
britannica-1911-lander-richard-lemon-and:
Lander, Richard Lemon and John, are the subjects of a 1911 Britannica entry on two English brothers. They were sons of an innkeeper at Truro in Cornwall. Richard went to the West Indies at age eleven in a merchant's service. He later served rich homes and toured the Cape Colony.

In 1825 Richard joined Hugh Clapperton on his second trip to West Africa. He stayed with Clapperton till his death near Sokoto in April 1827. Richard then made his way back to the coast through Yoruba. He brought Clapperton's journal with him, and it came out in 1829. His own tale of the trip came the next year. The state then sent him to trace the lower Niger.
britannica-1911-langton-john:
John Langton (died 1337) served England as chancellor. He ended as bishop of Chichester. A clerk in the royal chancery, he became chancellor in 1292. Church posts followed. Pope Boniface VIII blocked his bid for Ely in 1298. Edward I backed that bid. Langton even went to Rome for it.

He gave up the seal in 1302. Chichester came in 1305. He held the seal again under Edward II from 1307. The ordainers chose him in 1310. That link likely cost him office. Later he acted as go-between for the king. He served with Earl Thomas of Lancaster in 1318. He served again with rebel barons in 1321. He built the chapter house at Chichester.
britannica-1911-lawson-sir-john:
Sir John Lawson, who died in 1665, was a British sailor born at Scarborough. The 1911 Britannica article says he joined the parliament navy in 1642. He sailed with Penn to the Mediterranean in 1650. In the Dutch war he fought under Blake at the Downs and at the Kentish Knock. At Portland in 1653 his ship took heavy fire. He led in the North Sea and the Channel in the years that followed.

Lawson was a republican and an Anabaptist, and so a foe of Cromwell. He lost his post in 1656 and was jailed for a short time for plotting. When the Cromwell regime fell, his fleet ruled the Channel. His ships brought Charles the Second home to England, and the king made him a knight. He then fought the pirate states of Algiers. He was wounded to death at Lowestoft in the next Dutch war.
britannica-1911-lesley-john:
John Lesley (1527-1596) was a Scottish bishop and historian. Aberdeen gave him his master's degree. A church post came to him in 1538 by special leave. He was a natural son, and the leave let him hold it all the same. Law study at Poitiers, Toulouse, and Paris made him a doctor in 1553. Orders came in 1558.

At the Reformation he stood firm for the old faith. He faced Knox in public debate at Edinburgh in 1561. That year he helped fetch Queen Mary home to rule. A privy council seat and a law chair at Aberdeen followed. In 1565 he became a judge and abbot of Lindores. The see of Ross came next, in 1565. He helped revise the laws of Scotland. The Black Acts were printed in 1566, much by his care. Mary kept his loyalty through her fall.
britannica-1911-lightfoot-john:
Lightfoot, John is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an English divine and rabbinical scholar. Born at Stoke-upon-Trent on the twenty-ninth of March 1602, Lightfoot was educated at Christ's College, Cambridge, where he was reckoned the best speaker among the undergraduates. After posts at Repton and Norton-under-Hales he became domestic chaplain to Sir Rowland Cotton, an amateur Hebraist. His first book, a set of Christian and Judaical miscellanies, appeared at London in 1629.

The article follows his rise in church and university. He sat in the Westminster Assembly, where his journal of its proceedings is now a valued historical source. Though he often stood nearly alone, above all in the Erastian controversy, he shaped the debates. In 1643 he became master of Catharine Hall at Cambridge and rector of Much Munden, holding both posts until his death.
britannica-1911-lindley-john:
John Lindley (1799-1865) was an English botanist born at Catton near Norwich. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes his father ran a nursery garden there. His first book in 1819 rendered a French work on fruit into English. Works on roses and foxgloves followed in the next two years.

Work on a plant encyclopedia convinced him that a natural system beat the older one. He set that view out in books on British flora from 1829 onward. He held the chair of botany at University College London until 1860. He also edited plant journals and wrote many works on plant form and growing.
britannica-1911-linnell-john:
John Linnell was an English painter born in London in the late seventeen hundreds. His father carved and gilded for a trade, so the boy met artists early. At age ten he was drawing and selling chalk and pencil likenesses of sitters.

The 1911 Britannica entry traces his training step by step. A great master gave him his first lessons, and he spent a year in the house of a water color painter, with fellow pupils who grew famed. He won medals at the royal school for drawing and form. He also trained as an engraver, and in later life put out prints from the great frescoes of Rome and from royal picture rooms. At first he lived by small likenesses in paint.
britannica-1911-locke-john:
John Locke's long 1911 article is held here in a middle chunk, and the hosted text opens deep in the thought, not at the life. Matter and its traits fill these pages. First traits — bulk, shape, count, place, and motion — stay in things whether seen or not. Second traits, such as colour and sound, live in our sense of things.

Four kinds of accord ground all claim to know. One kind is sameness or lack of it among ideas. One is math-like links. One is traits that sit or fail to sit in one thing. One is plain being, apart from our sight of it. Sight at once, proof by steps, and sense grasp form the three roads to truth. Sense grasp sits lowest of the three. The chunk closes with the tale of Locke study: lives and letters drawn from the Shaftesbury papers and great libraries.
britannica-1911-lord-john:
John Lord (1810-1894) was an American writer and lecturer on history, and this 1911 Britannica entry follows his long career on the platform. He was born in Portsmouth, New Hampshire, the nephew of Nathan Lord, long president of Dartmouth College. He finished at Dartmouth in 1833 and at Andover seminary in 1837. On the way he taught school and toured New York and Ohio lecturing on the dark ages.

He worked as a lecturer for the American Peace Society and held brief pastor posts in Massachusetts and New York. About 1840 he made lecturing on history his trade, and he kept at it for fifty years, speaking widely in the United States and Britain. He made the mid-day lecture a success. From 1869 to 1876 he also lectured on history at Dartmouth. He made his home at Stamford, Connecticut, from 1854 until his death.
britannica-1911-lydgate-john:
John Lydgate, an English poet who lived from about 1370 to about 1451, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was born in the village of Lydgate, near Newmarket. His life was tied most of all to the abbey of Bury St Edmunds. He was most likely schooled at the school linked to that house of monks.

The article uses dates from his church career to fix his birth year. He was made sub-deacon in 1389, deacon in 1393, and priest in 1397. In his Testament he drew a lively picture of his boyhood self. He was a boy who robbed orchards, fought, and had little taste for early prayers. The piece also notes the high name he won for learning in his own time.
britannica-1911-macculloch-john:
John MacCulloch, a Scottish student of rocks who lived from 1773 to 1835, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in Guernsey and trained as a doctor at Edinburgh. He joined the army as a surgeon, then became chemist to the board of ordnance in 1803. Papers on Guernsey and the Channel Islands showed his gift in 1811.

That year he was sent to make wide surveys of the rocks of Scotland. Little had been done in that field, and he threw himself into the work. He rode and sailed the hard west coast isles and mapped them one by one. His report on them came out in 1819. He gave his great hoard of Scottish rocks and minerals to the Geological Society. He served as its president in 1816 and 1817.
britannica-1911-malalas-john:
John Malalas, who lived from about 491 to 578, was a Byzantine chronicler born at Antioch. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica says his surname is Syriac for orator. He wrote a chronicle in eighteen books. Its start and end are lost in the copy that survives. As it stands, it opens with the mythic history of Egypt. It closes with a campaign in Africa under Justinian's nephew.

Save for Justinian's age, the work has little worth as history. It lacks all sense of proportion and holds astonishing blunders. Malalas backs church and throne throughout. His tale centres on Antioch first, then on Constantinople. Its value lies in its audience and its tongue. It was the first chronicle written for monks and common folk. It uses the speech of the street, mixed with Latin and eastern words. That plain style won it wide use for centuries.
britannica-1911-marston-john:
John Marston, an English dramatist and satirist, was born about fifteen seventy five. He was the eldest son of John Marston of Coventry, a lecturer at the Middle Temple. His mother was the daughter of an Italian physician named Andrew Guarsi. That parentage may explain his ties with Italian literature, one critic notes. He entered Brasenose College, Oxford, in fifteen ninety two and took his degree.

Marston's father left him his law books and rooms in his will. The will regrets that the son would not follow the law as a profession. Marston wed Mary Wilkes, daughter of one of the royal chaplains. His first work was an erotic poem with satires, printed in fifteen ninety eight. A second book of eleven satires came out in the same year. Both books were burnt by order of the archbishop, the entry says.
britannica-1911-martin-john:
John Martin (1789-1854) was an English painter of vast biblical scenes, and his career is traced in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Haydon Bridge near Hexham, he was apprenticed to a coachbuilder, then placed with an Italian artist. He moved to London in 1806 and lived by teaching drawing and painting on china and glass.

The entry lists his rise through works such as Sadak in Search of the Waters of Oblivion, shown in 1812, and Joshua in 1815. His Belshazzar's Feast of 1821 drew both praise and attack and won a prize of two hundred pounds. Later came the Destruction of Herculaneum, the Creation, and the Eve of the Deluge, plus paid designs for Milton and the Bible.
britannica-1911-mayow-john:
Mayow, John is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an English chemist and doctor who worked far ahead of his age.
