Born in London in May 1643, Mayow entered Wadham College, Oxford, at fifteen and won a fellowship at All Souls in 1660. He joined the Royal Society in 1678 and died in London in 1679.

His Tractatus quinque of 1674 treats breathing, rickets, and the nitro-aerial spirit. Taking Boyle's proof that air is needed for burning, Mayow showed that fire feeds not on air as a whole but on a more active part of it. He held that the same part is drawn off by the lungs into the blood and that life cannot go on without it. A candle and a small animal shut in one vessel of air, he found, die in turn as it is used up.
britannica-1911-mcclintock-john:
John McClintock, an American Methodist church leader who lived from 1814 to 1870, is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Philadelphia, he studied at the University of Pennsylvania. He then taught maths, Latin, and Greek at Dickinson College in Carlisle. He spoke out against the Mexican War and against slavery.

In 1847 McClintock was charged with stirring a riot that freed enslaved people who had fled. He was cleared at trial, in a case that drew wide notice. Later he edited a Methodist journal, served churches in New York and Paris, and spoke for the North in the Civil War years. In 1867 he became the first head of Drew seminary in New Jersey. His large Bible reference work, made with James Strong, is also noted.
britannica-1911-michell-john:
John Michell is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Michell was an English thinker on nature and on rocks who lived from 1724 to 1793. He studied at Cambridge and became a fellow there. He held a chair in geology from 1762. Later he served as rector of Thornhill in Yorkshire.

The article praises his 1750 book on making strong magnets by art. He first made the torsion balance, a fine tool for small force tests. That tool later let Henry Cavendish weigh the earth. Michell also wrote a noted essay on the cause of earthquakes. It showed wide knowledge of rock layers in England and abroad. Other works deal with comets, stars, and measures of the earth.
britannica-1911-moore-john:
John Moore was a Scottish doctor and writer born at Stirling, son of a churchman. He took his degree in medicine at Glasgow, served with the army abroad, then kept up his studies in London and Paris. In Paris he was tied to the house of the British envoy.

The 1911 Britannica entry gives pride of place to his novel of a selfish rake. That book struck its age hard, and through the verse of Byron left a last mark on letters: Byron said his famed hero was meant to be that rake in verse. His other works hold less of a stamp, but his sketches of manners in five lands give rich stuff for the student of past life. He saw scenes of the French revolt at first hand in Paris.
britannica-1911-moore-sir-john:
Sir John Moore, a British general who lived from 1761 to 1809, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Glasgow, the son of John Moore, he meant from his early years to be a soldier. He learned the Prussian firing exercise and was always playing at taking Geneva in the field as a boy.

By the Duke of Hamilton's influence, Moore gained an ensigncy in the 51st Foot in 1776 and learned his drill at Minorca. In 1778 he was made captain lieutenant in a new regiment raised for the American War, and he stayed in America till the peace of 1783. In 1784 the Hamilton interest returned him to Parliament for a group of Scottish boroughs. Though he never spoke, he kept an independent line. He won the friendship of Pitt and of the Duke of York, and the respect of Burke.
britannica-1911-morton-john:
John Morton (about 1420 to 1500) was archbishop of Canterbury, a cardinal, and a statesman, and this 1911 Britannica entry traces his rise. His family had moved from Nottinghamshire into Dorset, and he was born at Bere Regis or Milborne St Andrew. He was schooled at the abbey of Cerne and at Balliol College, Oxford, took a law degree, and practised in the church courts in London.

He rose through council posts and church preferment under the Lancastrian party. He was present at the battle of Towton in 1461, on the losing side, and was attainted by the winning Yorkists for it. He lived with the exiled court of Margaret of Anjou at Bar until 1470. There he took an active hand in the diplomacy that joined Warwick and Clarence to the Lancastrian cause.
britannica-1911-narborough-sir-john:
Sir John Narborough was an English sea chief who died in sixteen eighty-eight. He came from an old Norfolk line. He won his first posts by brave deeds in a fight with the Dutch fleet. Peace then sent him to chart the South Seas.

He sailed in sixteen sixty-nine and passed through the straits of Magellan, but came home with his main goal unmet. War brought fresh fame at Solebay, and a knights rank soon came. He was sent to curb sea theft off Tripoli. By a bold night raid with gun boats he burnt ships in the port and forced a truce.
britannica-1911-nichol-john:
John Nichol, a Scots man of letters who lived from 1833 to 1894, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of an astronomer and was born on 8 September 1833. He was schooled at Glasgow and at Balliol College, Oxford, where he had a fine career. After a first class degree he stayed at Oxford as a coach.

At Oxford Nichol formed the Old Mortality Society with friends such as Dicey, Green, and Swinburne. In 1862 he became professor of English literature at Glasgow, where his sway was marked. He wrote the piece on American literature for the ninth edition of the Britannica in 1882. That piece shows his pungent style at its best, the text says. He left Glasgow for London in 1889. His best works are listed as a drama, Hannibal, a life of Byron, and books on Burns and Carlyle.
britannica-1911-norden-john:
John Norden, an English map and land writer born in fifteen forty eight, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the first English man to plan a full set of county tales and maps. His first work of weight was a view of Britain that began with Middlesex in fifteen ninety three. A hand copy holds notes by Lord Burleigh.

In fifteen ninety five he wrote a land tale of eight shires and isles for Queen Elizabeth. Next came a guide to his big view, then a tale of Hertfordshire. By his death he had done five more counties in hand script. Three were put in print long after he died. The entry marks the start of the county map tale as a set form in England.
britannica-1911-o-shanassy-sir-john:
Sir John O Shanassy, a statesman of the colony of Victoria, opens a rule life in the 1911 Britannica. Born in Ireland in eighteen eighteen, he was the son of a land surveyor. He wed in eighteen thirty nine and sailed that year for Australia. Farm work came first, then trade in the town of Melbourne. A church chief drew him into town and faith group work there.

When Victoria split from New South Wales in eighteen fifty one, he won a council seat. Gold finds at that same time set hard tests for the new rule. His force of mind put him at the front of its law work. He helped frame the charter for self rule in the colony. In eighteen fifty seven he formed a rule team as its premier.
britannica-1911-ogilby-john:
John Ogilby, a British writer who lived from 1600 to 1676, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born near Edinburgh, he found cash by a lucky venture to free his jailed father and bind himself to a dancing master. He went to Ireland with the Earl of Strafford as tutor to his children.

Strafford made him deputy master of the revels, and Ogilby built a small theatre in Dublin that did very well. The Civil War wrecked his fortunes, and he came back to England in 1646. At Cambridge, kind scholars taught him Latin, and he turned Virgil into English verse, a task that paid him well. He then learned Greek and issued translations of both the Iliad and the Odyssey. At the Restoration he was given the verse work for the coronation, and though the Great Fire took his goods, he rebuilt his house.
britannica-1911-ogilvie-john:
John Ogilvie (about 1580-1615) was a Jesuit who was put to death in Scotland, and this 1911 Britannica entry gives the bare facts of his end. He was born in Scotland and schooled mostly in Germany, where he joined the Society of Jesus. He was ordained a priest at Paris in 1613. That same year he went back to Scotland in disguise, dressed as a soldier, as an agent of his order.

In October 1614 he was seized at Glasgow. He was tried at Edinburgh and, though he defended himself with spirit, he was condemned to death. He was hanged on the last day of February 1615. The entry closes by pointing to sources for his story, including a report of his trial printed at Edinburgh in that year and later lives written by Catholic authors.
britannica-1911-oldham-john:
John Oldham, an English poet of sharp verse, gets a life in the 1911 Britannica. Born in Gloucestershire in sixteen fifty three, he was the son of a church man. He took his degree at Oxford in sixteen seventy four. School work at Croydon held him for three years of his youth. Verse he wrote there drew the Earl of Rochester down to meet him.

Panic from the tales of Titus Oates gave his rough gift its chance. His Satires on the Jesuits hit print in sixteen eighty one to great note. Hope of a free life by verse brought no pay from party chiefs. He took posts as a home tutor in great houses in turn. Smallpox cut his life short in sixteen eighty three, at age thirty.
britannica-1911-peile-john:
John Peile was an English student of tongues, born at a port town in the north in the mid eighteen hundreds. He was schooled at a famed school and at a college of Cambridge. A bright run there won him prizes, a fellowship, and a post as tutor in his own college.

He rose to read in the study of like tongues at the college town, the 1911 Britannica entry says, and then to head his college. He took a deep share in the push to give women a high schooling, and led a womens college as its head. His chief gift to his field was a primer that first brought two great German works on word roots to the English student. He died with a full tale of his college near done.
britannica-1911-pell-john:
John Pell is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an English scholar of numbers born in Sussex in sixteen ten. He entered a Cambridge college at the age of thirteen. He won fame for skill in tongues as well as in maths.

The entry tells how Dutch schools called him to teach maths at two towns. He then served as an envoy to Swiss lands for the English state. On his return he took church posts in Essex and held them for years. Love of maths hurt both his church rise and his purse, the entry says. He spent time in a debtors prison and died in London in sixteen eighty five.
britannica-1911-penry-john:
John Penry, who lived from 1559 to 1593, was a Welsh Puritan born in Brecknockshire. The 1911 Britannica article says he entered Peterhouse, Cambridge, in December 1580. He came there most likely a Catholic, but soon turned a firm Protestant with Puritan leanings. He took his first degree, then moved to Oxford for a second in 1586. He was licensed as a university preacher, without church ordination.

Penry was stirred by the poor state of faith in Wales. A law of 1562 had set up a Welsh Bible, but too few copies were printed to serve each parish. In 1587 he printed a plea for preaching in Wales. The archbishop had him jailed for a month for that rebuke. From 1588 he ran a roving press with the help of rich backers. It moved from town to town till it was seized at Manchester in 1589.
britannica-1911-perrot-sir-john:
Sir John Perrot (about 1527-1592) was lord deputy of Ireland. His mother was Mary Berkley, who later wed Thomas Perrot, a Pembrokeshire gentleman. Perrot was widely said to be a son of Henry VIII. He was placed in the household of the marquess of Winchester. That post brought him to the king's notice. He was knighted at the crowning of Edward VI.

Under Mary, Perrot spent a short time in prison for hiding heretics, his uncle among them. In spite of his Protestant faith, he gained the castle and lordship of Carew. At the start of Elizabeth's reign he was put in charge of the sea defence of South Wales. In 1570 he took, with some reluctance, the new post of lord president of Munster. In two years of hard campaigning he hunted down James Fitzmaurice Fitzgerald, who gave himself up in 1572.
britannica-1911-pettie-john:
Scottish painter John Pettie, born in Edinburgh in eighteen thirty nine, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In eighteen fifty two his family moved to East Linton. A portrait by the boy of the village carrier and his donkey won his father over to art as a career.

At sixteen he entered an art school in Edinburgh, under a noted teacher. He learned alongside a set of peers who later made names of their own. He first showed works drawn from the novels of Walter Scott. A work sent to London in eighteen sixty did well, and he settled there two years later. He became a full member of the Royal Academy in eighteen seventy four. The entry praises his speed, his colour, and his bright craft.
britannica-1911-phelps-edward-john:
Edward John Phelps is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born on the eleventh of July 1822 at Middlebury, Vermont, he was a lawyer and envoy of the United States. He took his degree at Middlebury College in 1840 and was admitted to the bar in 1843.

The article follows a career split between law and teaching. He held a treasury post in Washington, then practiced law in New York and Burlington. He helped found the national bar group and led it in 1880. From 1881 he held a chair of law at Yale. As envoy to Great Britain from 1885 to 1889 he served with credit. In 1893 he spoke for his land at a world court in Paris on the Bering Sea case. His closing speech took eleven days to give.
britannica-1911-philip-john:
John Philip, a British man sent to preach in South Africa, born in seventeen seventy five, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Kirkcaldy in Fife, he was the son of a school man of that town. He was put to learn the cloth trade, then was a clerk in a trade house at Dundee for three years. He then read for the church at a school in London.

In eighteen hundred and four he took a church post at Aberdeen. In eighteen eighteen he went with a peer on a tour of the posts of a great preach group in South Africa. His tale of that tour held that the Cape town men used the native folk in a way that drew strong blame.
britannica-1911-phillip-john:
John Phillip, a Scottish painter, is followed in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Aberdeen in 1817, he was an old soldier's son. Poor means set him first as errand boy to a tinsmith. Then a painter and glazier took him on as a learner. A local artist gave him some grounding in the craft of art.

At fifteen Phillip was painting portraits for pay in his town. A house call to mend a window changed his whole life path. The owner, Major Gordon, marked his love of the art there. Lord Panmure then sent him to London in 1836 for schooling. Royal Academy schools took him in as a student there. Portraits and Scots scenes kept him for the next ten years.
britannica-1911-phillips-john:
John Phillips (1800-1874) was an English geologist, and this 1911 Britannica entry follows his rise from museum keeper to national figure. He was born at Marden in Wiltshire on Christmas Day 1800. Both parents died while he was a child, and he was raised by his uncle William Smith, the famed map maker of English geology. Phillips travelled with Smith on his map work and learned the field at his side.

In 1824 he went with Smith to York and took posts arranging museums and lecturing in Yorkshire towns. He became keeper of the Yorkshire museum in 1825. When the British Association was founded at York in 1831, Phillips helped build its machinery and served as its first assistant secretary. Chairs at King's College London and work on the national geological survey followed, along with high honours from learned societies.
britannica-1911-pinkerton-john:
John Pinkerton was a Scots man of old lore, coins, and books who lived from seventeen fifty-eight to eighteen twenty-six. He was born at Edinburgh and bound as a law clerk there. A poem on a fort came out in his clerk years. In seventeen eighty-one he moved to London to live by his pen.

Songs and tales in verse came fast, plus a set of Scots songs. A peer showed that some old songs in that set were new work, and he owned to a share in them. His work on coins and on the first tale of Scotland still holds worth for the writs it holds.
britannica-1911-pinwell-george-john:
George John Pinwell, a British water colour painter who lived from 1842 to 1875, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Wycombe, he was educated at Heatherley's Academy. The entry places him in a small group of water colour painters that included Frederick Walker. Their style grew from drawing on wood for book illustration.

Pinwell is praised as one of the most pleasing book illustrators of his day. The article notes his poetic imagination, strong power of invention, and fine sense of colour. It says his early life held much hardship and his works are few, since he died young. Yet their promise was so great that a much higher place was thought likely had he lived.
britannica-1911-pond-john:
John Pond, an English astronomer royal born about seventeen sixty seven, was a London tradesman's son. His father made a fortune in trade in that city. Pond entered Trinity College, Cambridge, at the age of sixteen. He took no degree, since ill lungs forced a long stay abroad. In eighteen hundred he settled at Westbury near Bristol.

At Westbury, Pond began to fix star places with a fine instrument by Troughton. In eighteen o six he showed a change of form in the Greenwich mural quadrant. That proof led to new tools being brought in at the observatory. The head opens with the tail of an entry on another man, but the Pond account follows in full. His work set star measurement on a firmer footing for his age.
britannica-1911-popham-sir-john:
Sir John Popham (about 1531–1607) was an English judge born at Huntworth in Somerset. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows him from Balliol College, Oxford, and the Middle Temple into Parliament and high legal office. He was recorder of Bristol, Speaker in 1580, and attorney-general from 1581 until he became lord chief justice in 1592.

In that post he presided at the trials of Sir Walter Raleigh and Guy Fawkes. Late in life he threw his weight behind the planting of Virginia, helping win patents for the London and Plymouth companies. He also backed sending rogues and vagabonds abroad as a punishment. The Popham colony, led by his brother George, settled on the Kennebec river in 1607 but lasted only a short time. He died that same June and was buried at Wellington.
britannica-1911-porteous-john:
John Porteous is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was captain of the city guard of Edinburgh and died in the famed riots of 1736. His father was a tailor of that city, and Porteous had served in the army.

The article tells how a hanging sparked the clash. At the death of a liked smuggler in 1736, the guard fired on the crowd. Some were killed and many hurt. Porteous was tried and condemned to death for the shots. Word of a reprieve enraged the city. On the night of the seventh of September a masked band broke into the jail. They dragged him out and hanged him on a sign post in the street. No one was ever convicted for the killing.
britannica-1911-porter-fitz-john:
Fitz John Porter, an American soldier, was born at Portsmouth in New Hampshire in eighteen twenty two. He was the son of a naval officer and nephew of a famed frigate captain. He graduated at West Point in eighteen forty five and joined the artillery arm. In the Mexican War he won two brevets for gallant conduct in battle. He served at West Point as instructor and adjutant for six years.

Porter took part in the Utah expedition before the Civil War broke out. At the war's start he worked on staff duties in the east. He helped organize volunteers from Pennsylvania for the Union cause. On his own charge he let Missouri Unionists raise troops in their state. That step had a large effect on the fight for Missouri. Under McClellan he led a division, then a corps, in the Peninsular campaign.
britannica-1911-potter-john:
John Potter is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an English churchman who rose to become archbishop of Canterbury. Born near sixteen seventy four, he was the son of a cloth seller in Wakefield. He studied at Oxford and won a fellowship while still a young man.

The entry follows his work as a scholar of Greek and church history. It lists his books on Greek antiquities and his edition of an early church writer. It then traces his rise through church posts in Oxford and London. He became archbishop in seventeen thirty seven and held the post until his death ten years later.
britannica-1911-poynter-sir-edward-john:
Sir Edward John Poynter (1836-), an English painter, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The son of an architect, he was born in Paris in March 1836. He studied art in England and in Paris under Gleyre from 1856 to 1859. He showed his first picture at the Royal Academy in 1861.

The article tracks a swift rise. Two large pictures in 1869 won him election as an Associate of the Royal Academy. In 1876, the year of Atalanta's Race, he became a full member. He also worked freely in the arts of ornament, in fresco, mosaic, stained glass, pottery, and tile work. As a young man he designed panels for Gothic cabinets. Firms took his cartoons for stained glass, and he made thirty designs for a great abbey church. His drawings on wood filled a famed Bible gallery.
britannica-1911-rich-john:
John Rich, an English actor called the father of English pantomime, is covered in a 1911 Britannica life story. He lived from 1692 to 1761 and was the son of the Drury Lane manager Christopher Rich. John opened the new playhouse in Lincoln's Inn Fields, left half built by his father.

In 1716, under the stage name Lun, Rich first played Harlequin there. The show grew into a yearly pantomime and let him rival the stronger Drury Lane troupe. He opened Covent Garden in 1733, with mixed luck at first. A fine season came when Garrick joined him in 1746. Verse by Garrick praises Rich's mute art, which spoke through each limb.
britannica-1911-roby-henry-john:
Henry John Roby (1830-) was an English scholar of classics and Roman law, and his career is set out in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Tamworth in 1830, he studied at St John's College, Cambridge, where he was senior classic in 1853 and a fellow the next year. He later taught law at University College, London.

The entry notes his work as a commissioner of endowed schools and his five years in Parliament for the Eccles division of Lancashire. His best known book was a grammar of Latin from Plautus to Suetonius, rich in quoted examples. His chief works, though, dealt with Roman law, above all his books on Justinian's Digest and on Roman private law.
britannica-1911-rodgers-john:
John Rodgers (1771–1838) was an American sailor, born in Harford county, Maryland, on 11 July 1771. He joined the United States navy when it was set up in 1798. He was second in command to Commodore James Barron on the trip against the Barbary pirates. In 1805 he took Barron's place in command. That year he brought both Tunis and Tripoli to terms, and then came home to America.

In 1811 Rodgers held command of the frigate President, off Annapolis. Word came that a British frigate off Sandy Hook had pressed an American seaman from his ship. Rodgers was sent to sea to guard American trade. He may also have had word, by mouth, to strike back for such acts, a chief cause of the War of 1812. On 16 May 1811 he sighted the British sloop Little Belt and gave chase.
britannica-1911-roebuck-john:
John Roebuck, an English inventor born at Sheffield in seventeen eighteen, was the son of a thriving maker. He went to grammar school and to an academy at Northampton. He then studied medicine at Edinburgh, where lectures in chemistry drew him in. He took his medical degree at Leiden in seventeen forty two. He set up as a doctor at Birmingham but gave much time to chemistry.

In seventeen forty six Roebuck brought in lead chambers to condense acid in making sulphuric acid. With Samuel Garbett he built an acid works near Edinburgh in seventeen forty nine. For some years the pair held the field alone. He took no patents in time, so others soon used his methods. He then turned to iron and founded the Carron works in seventeen sixty.
britannica-1911-rolland-john:
John Rolland, a Scottish poet at work about 1560, is the subject of a short entry in the 1911 Britannica. He seems to have been a priest of the Glasgow diocese, known at Dalkeith in 1555. He wrote two poems, the Court of Venus and a rendering of the Seven Sages. The first was printed by John Ros in 1575, though it may have been written before 1560.

The Seven Sages was turned from a Scots prose version at the hint of an aunt who found his courtly tale dull. It was printed in 1578 and often reprinted in the early 1600s. The entry gives the later print history of both works, with editions of 1837 and 1884. It also weighs a claim that Rolland wrote the Thrie Priestis of Peblis. The verdict is firm: no scrap of proof backs it.
britannica-1911-ross-john:
John Ross, chief of the Cherokee Indian Nation, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Of Scotch and Indian descent, he was born among the Cherokees in Georgia in seventeen ninety. He was also known by the name Kooeskoowe. In the eighteen twenties he led the Cherokee national committee.

In July eighteen twenty seven he presided over the Cherokee constituent assembly. Under the constitution that body drafted, he became principal chief the next year. He held that post until his death. In eighteen thirty he asked the Supreme Court to restrain Georgia from enforcing its laws in Cherokee land. The court dismissed his suit for lack of jurisdiction.
britannica-1911-ross-sir-john:
Sir John Ross, a British rear admiral and Arctic rover born in seventeen seventy seven, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Son of a church man in Wigtonshire, he joined the Royal Navy in seventeen eighty six. He served in the inland sea and then in the Channel. In time he led a Swedish fleet as captain.

In eighteen eighteen he was given charge of an Arctic trip set up by the state. It was the first of a new run of tries to find a north west sea road. That trip found not much that was new. It hurt his name in the north trade. In eighteen twenty nine a rich backer let him sail once more. That trip was gone four years. It won great gains for the map and for science. The entry shows a name restored by grit.
britannica-1911-routh-edward-john:
Edward John Routh is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Quebec on the twentieth of January 1831, he was an English worker in maths. He came to England at the age of eleven. After study in London he entered Peterhouse, Cambridge, in 1851.

The article centres on his fame as a coach of young talent. In the great maths test of 1854 he came first, ahead of Maxwell. He then spent his life teaching at Cambridge. In thirty years some 700 pupils passed through his hands. Five hundred of them took top honours, a share the text calls unmatched. For twenty two years in a row the top man was trained by him. His books on motion and statics are also named.
britannica-1911-row-john:
John Row is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Row was a Scottish reformer, born near Stirling about 1525. He trained at St Andrews and practised as an advocate in the church court. In 1550 he was sent to Rome on business for the archbishop of St Andrews.

High authorities in Rome marked him out, and in 1558 he was named papal nuncio. His charge was to inquire into the spread of heresy in Scotland. That inquiry changed his own faith instead. Under Knox's preaching he joined the reformers in 1560. He became a minister at Kennoway and then at Perth. He was one of six men who drew up the Confession of Faith and the First Book of Discipline. The entry tells a neat reversal: the pope's own investigator became a builder of the Reformed church.
britannica-1911-rushworth-john:
John Rushworth, the note taker of a revolt, is tracked in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born about 1612, he was a Northumberland squire's son of Acklington. Law was his trade, and Berwick took him as its solicitor in 1638. Lincoln's Inn called him to the bar in the year 1647. His bent was to sit in on each great public act.

Rushworth took shorthand notes at trials and council boards alike. In 1640 the House of Commons took him as a clerk's help. He sat on duty when Charles came to seize five members. His notes of that day's speech the king had printed at once. He rode as go-between of king and parliament in the war. Fairfax took him as secretary, and Naseby saw his pen at work.
britannica-1911-rutledge-john:
John Rutledge, an American jurist and politician who lived from 1739 to 1800, gets a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. Born in Charleston, South Carolina, he studied law in London and began practice at home in 1761. He sat in the Stamp Act Congress of 1765 and in the Continental Congress. In 1776 he chaired the framing of the state constitution and became the first president, or governor, of South Carolina.

He quit that post in 1778, then served as governor again till 1782. At the federal convention of 1787 he urged that the president and judges be chosen by the Senate. Named chief justice of the Supreme Court in 1795, he presided for one term, but the Senate refused to confirm him. His mind failed late that year, and he died at Charleston in 1800.
britannica-1911-simon-sir-john:
Sir John Simon lived from 1816 to 1904 and was an English surgeon and reformer. The 1911 Britannica life stresses his work for clean towns and public health. He was born in London in October 1816 to a stock exchange man. Both his grandfathers were French exiles who traded in England in trade. His parents both lived to near a hundred years of age.

His father meant him for surgery from the boy's youth on. In October 1833, just short of seventeen, he began to study medicine. He trained under Joseph Henry Green at St Thomas's hospital in London. Green was famed both as a surgeon and as a friend of Coleridge. Simon rose to teach anatomy and to serve as a hospital surgeon.
britannica-1911-sinclair-sir-john:
Sinclair, Sir John, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of a Scots writer. Born at Thurso Castle on the 10th of May 1754, he came of the Caithness earls. He read at Edinburgh, Glasgow, and Trinity College at Oxford. He joined the Scots bar and the English bar, but never practised.

In 1780 he entered the Commons for Caithness in the north. His Commons career ran, with few breaks, until the year 1811. He set up a society at Edinburgh to lift British wool. He was key to the birth of the Board of Agriculture. He was also first president of that board in its work. His book on the public revenue came out in 1784. His plan for state bills saved wide ruin in 1793.
britannica-1911-skinner-john:
John Skinner was a Scottish author who lived from seventeen twenty one to eighteen o seven. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Balfour in Aberdeenshire, the son of a parish schoolmaster, he studied at Aberdeen. He was meant for the Presbyterian ministry but took Episcopal orders instead.

Skinner took charge at Longside in seventeen forty two, just before hard times. After the Jacobite rising of seventeen forty five, his church was burnt down. His house was looted, and he served his flock in secret for years. In seventeen fifty three he spent six months in jail for his work. Burns praised his song Tullochgorum as the best Scotch song ever made.
britannica-1911-slidell-john:
John Slidell, an American lawmaker and envoy from Louisiana, fills a 1911 Britannica life. Born in New York City in seventeen ninety three, he took his degree at Columbia in eighteen ten. He tried trade, then law, and rose at the bar in New Orleans. He sat in the House for two years as a states rights man. President Polk then sent him on a hush trip to Mexico.

That trip failed, but he won a Senate seat and held it through the fifties. When Louisiana left the Union he went south as an envoy to France. Sea men from a Union ship seized him off a British steamer, a famed case of the war. Freed, he sought French aid for the South and failed. He died in London in eighteen seventy one.
britannica-1911-smart-john:
Smart, John, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of an English painter of miniatures. Born in Norfolk about 1740, he was a pupil of Cosway. He rose to lead the Incorporated Society of Artists as a chief officer. His work was shown with that society for years.

In 1788 he went to India and won many portrait orders there. He settled in London in 1797 and died there in 1811. The entry calls him a small man of plain habits and quiet faith. His art is set apart from his master's showy style. Its hues are quiet and grey, with flesh tints worked with fine care. His grasp of the body's build gave his portraits rare strength.
britannica-1911-smeaton-john:
John Smeaton (1724-1792) was an English civil engineer born at Austhorpe Lodge, near Leeds, on 8 June 1724. He went to Leeds grammar school and showed a gift for tools as a boy. In his teens he built a lathe of his own. He left his father's law office to train with a maker of fine instruments. In 1750 he set up in business for himself.

Smeaton made better tools for use at sea and in star study. He also ran tests on mills and machines driven by water and wind. His paper on that work won the Copley medal of the Royal Society in 1759. The article traces the start of a long and busy career.
britannica-1911-smith-john:
John Smith lived from 1579 to 1631 and led the English colony in Virginia. He is best known as Captain John Smith, the entry notes at once. The 1911 Britannica life opens in Willoughby in Lincolnshire, his birth place. His father was a well off tenant farmer on a lord's estate. Smith himself split his life into five clear parts or spells.

As a boy he went to free schools at Alford and at Louth. His parents died in April 1596, when he was in his teens. Left with means he could not yet guide, he cared little for them. His mind was set on brave deeds from the very first. He sold his books and goods and sought to slip off to sea.
britannica-1911-smybert-john:
John Smybert, a Scottish American artist who lived from 1684 to 1751, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica article. He was born at Edinburgh and studied under Sir James Thornhill. In 1728 he sailed to America with Bishop Berkeley. He meant to teach fine arts at a college Berkeley planned in Bermuda.

The college was never founded, so Smybert settled in Boston and wed there in 1730. In 1731 he painted Bishop Berkeley and His Family, a group of eight now at Yale. His portraits list Jonathan Edwards, Peter Faneuil, and Governor John Endecott. Works by him are held by Harvard, Yale, and Bowdoin. His son Nathaniel, also a painter, died at age twenty two.
britannica-1911-smyth-john:
John Smyth, who lived from about 1570 to 1612, was an English nonconformist divine called the Se Baptist. The 1911 Britannica entry follows him from Christ College at Cambridge to a Yorkshire vicar post. In 1600 he became lecturer for the city of Lincoln by election. Two years later he was stripped of that post as a factious preacher.

Two volumes of his Lincoln sermons came out in 1603 and 1605 in print. While at work on them he drew close to the Separatist circles of Scrooby and Gainsborough. He joined the Gainsborough church and became its pastor in that movement. The entry opens the tale of a founder of English Baptist life.
britannica-1911-speed-john:
John Speed (1552–1629) is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an English historian and map maker. The son of a London tailor, he followed his father's trade and joined the Merchant Taylors Company in 1580. Help from Sir Fulke Greville let him give up the trade and spend his days on old history.

In 1611 his Theatre of the Empire of Great Britaine came out, a set of fifty four maps of parts of England, with notes fixed to each map. He had help from Christopher Saxton, John Norden and William White. The same year he put out a history of Great Britain from the Roman conquests to King James. Great scholars of the day lent him their books and coins. He also wrote works on the lines of descent in the Bible, often bound in front of copies of it.
britannica-1911-spottiswoode-john:
John Spottiswoode, archbishop of St Andrews and a historian of Scotland, lived from 1565 to 1639. His life is told in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the eldest son of a minister of Calder and was educated at Glasgow. He took his degree in 1581 and followed his father in the parish of Calder in 1583.

He first stood out as a strong man of the strict Presbyterian party. In time he came to doubt the worth of strict parity in the Church. He held that church and state both gained by good terms with the king. So he worked with James to curb the powers of the Kirk and to shape the Scottish church more like that of England. In 1610 he led the assembly that ended presbytery. In 1615 he became archbishop of St Andrews, and in 1633 he crowned Charles the First.
britannica-1911-stainer-sir-john:
Sir John Stainer, who lived from 1840 to 1901, was an English composer and organist born at Southwark. The 1911 Britannica article says he was born on the sixth of June 1840. His father, a parish schoolmaster, taught him organ and the reading of music. In 1847 the boy entered the choir of Saint Paul's Cathedral. He stayed nine years and at times played the organ in a pinch. Posts at small churches came in his last choir year.

In 1860 Stainer went to Magdalen College, Oxford, and next year became university organist. He raised the Magdalen choir to a rare pitch of skill. Degrees in arts and in music followed in quick order. In 1872 he took the organ at Saint Paul's and lifted its choral music near to perfection. Later posts made him a judge of music in training colleges across the land.
britannica-1911-stark-john:
John Stark, who lived from 1728 to 1822, was an American soldier born in New Hampshire. The 1911 Britannica article says he was born on the twenty-eighth of August 1728. In 1752 Indians seized him, and Massachusetts paid his ransom. In the Seven Years' War he served under Robert Rogers as lieutenant and then captain. He fought at Lake George and in the failed attack on Ticonderoga. At the start of the war for independence he raised a regiment.

As colonel, Stark served well at Bunker Hill and in the New Jersey campaign. Passed over for promotion, he quit in March 1777. New Hampshire soon gave him a brigade of militia. On the sixteenth of August he beat two parts of Burgoyne's army near Bennington. That win did much to force the surrender of Burgoyne. Congress thanked him and made him a brigadier in the main army.
britannica-1911-sterling-john:
John Sterling, a British author who lived from 1806 to 1844, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Kames Castle in Bute, of a Scots family long settled in Ireland. His father Edward wrote fierce letters to The Times signed Vetus. Those letters gave that paper its nickname of the Thunderer.

John studied at Glasgow and then at Trinity College, Cambridge. There he shone in debate and joined the club called the Apostles. His friends there, Maurice and Trench, stayed close for life. He left Cambridge with no degree, set on a life of letters. With Maurice he bought the Athenaeum journal in 1828, though the venture lost money. The entry frames him through his kin and his circle as much as through his own pen.
britannica-1911-stewart-john:
John Stewart, a British traveller known as Walking Stewart, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in London in seventeen forty nine of humble parents, he had a wild school career. In seventeen sixty three he entered the service of the East India Company at Madras. He soon left that post.

He became interpreter to Hyder Ali and later served as a general in his army. He then served the nabob of Arcot as chief minister and grew rich in that role. After that he travelled widely through India, Persia, and Abyssinia. Those long journeys on foot earned him the nickname by which he is still known.
britannica-1911-still-john:
John Still is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an English bishop born near fifteen forty three at Grantham. He studied at a Cambridge college and rose to its fellowship young. He took holy orders and climbed the ranks of church and school.

The entry lists his chairs, livings, and headships at two great colleges. He twice served as vice head of his university in hard years. In fifteen ninety three he rose to bishop of Bath and Wells. Lead mines on his church lands left him a large fortune at death. A famed early English comedy of fun has long been tied to his name.
britannica-1911-stokesley-john:
John Stokesley, an English church leader born near 1475, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life story. He was born at Colly Weston and became a fellow of Magdalen College, Oxford. In 1498 he was made head of Magdalen Hall. Soon after 1509 he joined the royal council as chaplain to Henry the Eighth.

Stokesley went to France and Italy in 1529 and 1530 as an envoy. His task was to win views from foreign schools in favor of the king's divorce. In 1530 he became bishop of London. He baptized the princess Elizabeth in 1533. His last years were marred by fights with Archbishop Cranmer. He held fast to the old church teachings and died in 1539.
britannica-1911-stoughton-john:
John Stoughton, an English Nonconformist divine who lived from 1807 to 1897, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Norwich, he was schooled there and at Highbury Congregational College. His father was an Anglican and his mother a Quaker. He became minister at Windsor in 1833 and at Kensington in 1843.

In 1856 Stoughton was elected chair of the Congregational Union. From 1872 to 1884 he taught historical theology at New College in Hampstead. He was no fighter in debate, but he did sound work in church history. His books trace church and state under the Stuarts and the church in England across two centuries. He also arranged a conference on work shared by Anglicans and dissenters. Popular books on Luther and on the reformers of Italy and Spain are also noted.
britannica-1911-stow-john:
John Stow (about 1525-1605), an English historian and collector of antiquities, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of a London tailor and was born in the parish of St Michael in Cornhill. His parents were poor: the rent for house and garden came to just a few shillings a year. As a boy he fetched the family's milk each morning from a farm.

He learned his father's trade but may not have practised it long. About 1560 he began the work his name rests on. He came to know the leading antiquaries of his time, among them William Camden. In 1561 he published an edition of the works of Chaucer, with matter never printed before. Four years later came his summary of the English chronicles, a book reprinted again and again in his lifetime.
britannica-1911-strachan-john:
John Strachan (1778-1867) was the first bishop of Toronto, and this 1911 Britannica entry follows his path from Aberdeen to Canada. He was born at Aberdeen in Scotland, the son of an overseer in the granite quarries. His father died in an accident in 1792, and the boy had to rely on himself and help his mother. By teaching and a bursary he reached the university of Aberdeen and took his degree.

He attended some divinity classes and formed lasting friendships with fellow students. In 1799 he emigrated to Canada, recommended to a Kingston notable as a tutor. Strachan went to Canada a Presbyterian. His company there, though, was almost wholly Episcopalian, including the one clergyman of the district. The entry goes on to show how that setting shaped the churchman he became.
britannica-1911-strachey-sir-john:
Sir John Strachey is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Strachey was a British official in India, born in London in 1823. He entered the Bengal civil service in 1842. Over a long career he held many high posts in Indian government.

The article follows that career post by post. He led an inquiry into the cholera outbreak of 1861 and later headed a lasting health board. In Oudh he worked to repair unjust land seizures after the Mutiny. As finance member he cut salt duties and helped end the inland customs line. A dispute over the cost of the Afghan War forced his resignation. The entry closes with his books on India and his death in 1907.
britannica-1911-strype-john:
John Strype, an English historian and biographer who lived from 1643 to 1737, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born in Houndsditch, London, in November 1643, he was the son of a Brabant family that fled religious persecution. He went to school at St Paul's and then to Jesus College, Cambridge. He took his first degree in 1665 and a master's degree in 1669.

Strype spent his working life as a clergyman in Essex parishes. He served at Theydon Bois and then at Leyton, where he preached for the rest of his life. In 1711 Archbishop Tenison gave him the sinecure of West Tarring in Sussex. He also lectured at Hackney for many years, from 1689 to 1724. He died at Hackney in December 1737, aged ninety-four, and was buried at Leyton.
britannica-1911-stuart-sir-john:
John Stuart, who lived from 1759 to 1815, was a British army general. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his long war service. Born in Georgia, he was the son of a royal officer there. He joined the Foot Guards in 1778 and sailed for America at once.

Stuart fought in the American war and later in the Low Countries. He won praise for his brigade work at Alexandria in 1801. In Italy he took short command against the French in 1806. He landed in Calabria and beat a French force at Maida. That win earned him a count title from the Palermo court. Parliament also voted him its thanks for the stroke.
britannica-1911-stubbs-john:
John Stubbs, an English pamphleteer who lived from about 1543 to 1591, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in Norfolk and read at Trinity College, Cambridge. After law study at Lincoln's Inn he settled at Thelveton. His views were Puritan in cast.

Stubbs loathed the talks for a marriage between Queen Elizabeth and the duke of Anjou. In 1579 he put his case in a pamphlet called the Gaping Gulf. The book warned that another French marriage would swallow England whole. Its sale was banned, and Stubbs, his printer, and his publisher were tried at Westminster. All three were sentenced to lose their right hands. The printer was pardoned, but the sentence fell on Stubbs and his publisher. With his hand cut off, Stubbs waved his hat with the left. He cried God Save the Queen before he fainted away.
britannica-1911-suckling-sir-john:
Sir John Suckling (1609-1642) was an English poet, and this 1911 Britannica entry follows his short, bright career. He was born at Whitton in Middlesex and baptized in February 1609. His father, also Sir John, had held high household and state posts under James the First and sat in Parliament under Charles the First. The father built a large fortune, of which the poet became master at eighteen.

He went to Trinity College, Cambridge, in 1623 and entered Gray's Inn in 1627. He moved among wits and poets, Carew, Lovelace, and Davenant among them. In 1628 he left London to travel in France and Italy, came home in 1630, and was knighted. In 1631 he volunteered for the force raised to serve under Gustavus Adolphus in Germany. He was back at Whitehall by May 1632, having seen battle in that short service.
britannica-1911-sullivan-john:
John Sullivan is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Somersworth, New Hampshire, on the eighteenth of February 1740, he was a soldier and public leader in the young United States. He read law and sat in the New Hampshire assembly in 1774.

The article follows his war service in close detail. He led the raid that took Fort William and Mary in December 1774. As a general he served at Boston, in Canada, and at Long Island, where he was taken. Freed, he fought at Trenton, Brandywine, and Germantown. In 1779 he beat the Iroquois and their allies at Newtown. He burned their towns and crops, and won the thanks of Congress.
britannica-1911-tobin-john:
John Tobin, who lived from 1770 to 1804, was an English playwright born at Salisbury. The 1911 Britannica article says he was born on the twenty-eighth of January 1770, the son of a merchant. He was schooled at Bristol Grammar School and worked in London as a solicitor. From 1789 he gave all his spare time to writing plays. Thirteen plays were turned down in a row. At last, in 1803, a slight farce of his was staged.

In 1804 Tobin sent his fourteenth play, The Honey Moon, to Drury Lane. Sure it would fail, he left London to mend his health. Word that it had been taken came too late. Sick with consumption, he sailed for the West Indies in December 1804. He died on the first day of the voyage. The play was staged the next year and won great success.
britannica-1911-torrey-john:
John Torrey lived from 1796 to 1873 and was an American botanist. The 1911 Britannica life opens in New York, where he was born in August 1796. At age fifteen his father took a post at a prison in Greenwich. There the boy met Amos Eaton, a pioneer of natural history in America. From Eaton he learned the first rules of botany and of minerals.

In 1815 he began the study of medicine and qualified in 1818. Next year he issued a catalogue of plants near New York city. In 1824 came the first volume of his Flora of the Northern States. That same year he took the chair of chemistry at West Point. Three years later he taught chemistry and botany to surgeons in New York.
britannica-1911-trelawny-edward-john:
Edward John Trelawny, an English sailor and friend of Shelley and Byron who lived from 1792 to 1881, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in London, he was the son of an army officer. After a short term in the navy he shipped for India, then left his ship at Bombay. He led a wild life in India for some years, then came home about 1813.

Early in 1822 Trelawny met Shelley and Byron at Pisa and was with them near each day. He oversaw the recovery and burning of the body of Shelley after the drowning of July 1822. Tale says he snatched the heart of Shelley from the flames. In 1823 he sailed with Byron for Greece to aid its war for freedom. He later wed the sister of a Greek chief and was near killed at a fort on Parnassus.
britannica-1911-trenchard-sir-john:
Trenchard, Sir John, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of an English statesman. Born at Lytchett Matravers on the 30th of March 1640, he came of an old Dorset house. He was schooled at New College, Oxford, in his youth. In 1679 he entered the Commons as member for Taunton.

He joined the men who sought to bar the duke of York from the throne. Held in July 1683 over the Rye House plot, he was freed for lack of proof. When Monmouth landed in 1685 he fled abroad for two years. A pardon won by William Penn let him come home. William the Third knighted him and made him chief justice of Chester. In 1692 he rose to secretary of state.
britannica-1911-trevor-sir-john:
Sir John Trevor, an English politician, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in sixteen twenty six, he was a son of Sir John Trevor of Trevelyn in Denbighshire. His father sat in parliaments under two kings and under the Commonwealth. He also served on the council of state in that period.

The family held other noted members, the entry explains. One uncle was a naval officer who was knighted early in the century. Another uncle was the judge who ruled for the Crown in the famed ship money case. That judge was later impeached and fined. Against that backdrop Sir John entered Parliament himself.
britannica-1911-tulloch-john:
John Tulloch lived from 1823 to 1886 and was a Scottish church scholar. The 1911 Britannica life begins at Bridge of Earn in Perthshire. He studied at St Andrews and at Edinburgh for his degrees. In 1845 he became minister of St Paul's church in Dundee. Four years later he moved to Kettins in Strathmore for six years.

In 1854 he took charge of St Mary's College at St Andrews. There he taught the study of God and the defence of faith. His prize essay on theism came out at the same time. He lectured on faiths of the world in a new way. Doctrine, he taught, grows through time and is not fixed. Pupils loved his class room work from the very start.
britannica-1911-tyler-john:
John Tyler is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Tyler was the tenth president of the United States, born in Virginia in 1790. His father had been governor of Virginia and a federal judge. The family claimed kinship with the rebel Wat Tyler, a claim the entry says cannot be proved.

Tyler entered the College of William and Mary as a boy and graduated in 1807. He was admitted to the bar two years later. Public life began in 1811 with a seat in the Virginia House of Delegates. He served five years there and sat on the council of state. In 1813 he raised a company of men for the defence of Richmond. The article opens the career of a president who reached the White House by a path no one had planned.
britannica-1911-tyndall-john:
John Tyndall is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Tyndall was a British thinker on nature who lived from 1820 to 1893. He was born in County Carlow in Ireland. With Darwin and Huxley, his name is tied to the fight for modern science in general life. For years he stood to most English readers as the model physics professor.

The article calls him largely a self made man with no early advantages. He worked in land survey posts in Ireland and England. He then worked as a railway engineer and as a college teacher. In 1848 he went to Marburg in Germany. By hard study he gained his doctorate in two years. His first new work dealt with magnetism and its weaker reverse form. That work made his name in the science world by 1852.
britannica-1911-varley-john:
John Varley is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an English painter in water colour born in London in seventeen seventy eight. His father, a man of science, set him to work with a silver smith. The boy chafed at the trade and quit it when his father died.

The entry tells how tours to sketch great buildings trained his eye and hand. Wild hill scenes in North Wales won his heart on his first trip there. He showed his first work at a royal show in seventeen ninety eight. He helped found a new society for water colour art soon after. More than forty of his works hung in its first show.
britannica-1911-veitch-john:
Veitch, John is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Scottish writer. The son of a Peninsular veteran, he was born at Peebles on the twenty-fourth of October 1829 and educated at Edinburgh University. He assisted two famous teachers in turn, Sir William Hamilton and Alexander Campbell Fraser. In 1860 he took the chair of logic and rhetoric at St Andrews.

In philosophy he was an intuitionist, and he dismissed the idealist arguments with some abruptness. That bluntness cost him much of the influence his force of character had won. He died on the third of September 1894. The article says he will be remembered chiefly for his work on Border literature and antiquities. It lists his translations of Descartes, his poems, and his History and Poetry of the Scottish Border.
britannica-1911-walter-john:
John Walter, born in seventeen thirty eight or nine, was the founder of The Times newspaper in London. From his father's death until seventeen eighty one he ran a good trade as a coal merchant. He helped set up a Coal Exchange in London. Then he turned to insurance work at Lloyd's, speculated too far, and failed. He had bought a patent for printing from blocks of whole words.

In seventeen eighty four Walter bought an old printing office in Blackfriars. At first he printed books only from that base. On the first of January seventeen eighty five he launched a small daily paper. At its nine hundred fortieth number it took the name The Times. In seventeen eighty nine he was tried for libel on the duke of York. He was fined, jailed for a year, and put in the pillory.
britannica-1911-webster-john:
John Webster was an English dramatist whose known work runs from 1602 to 1624 in the records. The 1911 Britannica entry admits that nothing sure is known of him outside those dates. Henslow diary notes his hand in three plays in the year 1602 alone. In 1624 he wrote the city pageant for London as a merchant tailor.

Seven plays bear his name, three of them his alone by the title pages. A lost tragedy with Ford is mourned as a treasure gone by chance. Additions to Marston Malcontent in 1604 show his hand at other men work. The entry builds a master of dark tragedy from scraps and title pages.
britannica-1911-wesley-john:
John Wesley, an English church leader who lived from 1703 to 1791, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life story. He was born at Epworth Rectory on June 17, 1703. He was the fifteenth child of Samuel and Susanna Wesley. His mother trained him as a boy, and the home burned down in 1709.

Wesley went to Charterhouse school and then to Christ Church, Oxford, in June 1720. His health was poor and he fell into debt, yet he used his time well. The piece cites his early diary and a strict plan of study from 1722. It also notes how books by Thomas a Kempis and Jeremy Taylor shaped him in 1725.
britannica-1911-weyman-stanley-john:
Stanley John Weyman, an English novelist, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica article. He was born at Ludlow in Shropshire on August 7, the son of a solicitor. The text prints two birth years for him, so the year is left open here. He was schooled at Shrewsbury and at Christ Church, Oxford.

Weyman took his degree in modern history in 1877 and was called to the bar in 1881. He practiced law for eight years on the Oxford circuit. He then won his name as a novelist with a run of romances set in French history. The House of the Wolf came in 1889, then A Gentleman of France and Under the Red Robe. Later novels list Shrewsbury, Sophia, and Count Hannibal.
britannica-1911-whethamstede-john:
English abbot John Whethamstede, who died in fourteen sixty five, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was son of Hugh Bostock and was born at Wheathampstead in Hertfordshire. His name came from that birthplace. In early life he entered Saint Albans Abbey, and in fourteen twenty he was chosen its abbot.

In England his time went mainly to lawsuits to defend abbey property and rights. He attended a council at Pavia in fourteen twenty three. He resigned his post in fourteen forty, but became abbot a second time in fourteen fifty one. He was a keen and able abbot who much improved the abbey buildings. He was a friend of Duke Humphrey of Gloucester and helped him gather a famed set of books. He was himself a writer.
britannica-1911-whitgift-john:
John Whitgift is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Great Grimsby in Lincolnshire about 1530, he was the eldest son of a merchant. He became an English archbishop and a hard foe of the Puritans.

The article traces his climb at Cambridge. He held chairs of divinity, led two colleges, and helped frame the rules of the whole school in 1570. In print and in debate he fought Thomas Cartwright over church customs. He had Cartwright stripped of his posts in 1570 and 1571. Posts as dean of Lincoln and bishop of Worcester followed. In August 1583 he rose to archbishop of Canterbury. There he gave the church of the new age its lasting shape.
britannica-1911-wilkinson-john:
John Wilkinson was an American general whose western dealings fill the hosted text. The passage opens with his service as clothier general from 1779 to 1781. In 1784 he settled near the Falls of the Ohio at Louisville. There he grew rich as a merchant and farmer with wide sway.

He backed a split of Kentucky from the Union in those years. In 1787 he swore loyalty to Spain and took a Spanish pension. Spanish records knew him by the code name Number Thirteen. At the same time he rose to command of the regular army. The account stresses this double game at length.
britannica-1911-witherspoon-john:
John Witherspoon, a Scottish-American divine and teacher who lived from 1723 to 1794, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Gifford in East Lothian, the son of a minister of the Scots church. He traced his line on his mother's side to John Welch and to John Knox. He took his degree at Edinburgh in 1739 and his divinity course in 1743.

He was licensed to preach in 1743 and ordained at Beith in 1745. His books hit at faults in the church and mocked the moderate party. In 1757 he became pastor at Paisley. He was sued for libel for a printed rebuke to some of his flock, and a court made him pay damages, which his people raised for him. He said no to calls from Dublin and Rotterdam.
britannica-1911-wolcot-john:
John Wolcot (1738-1819), an English satirist and poet known as Peter Pindar, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of a surgeon in Devonshire and was schooled at free schools in Cornwall and in France. For seven years he was bound to his uncle, a surgeon, and he took a medical degree at Aberdeen in 1767.

In 1769 he was ordained and sailed to Jamaica with the new governor, whose household he served. He became a rector there, but when his patron died in 1772 he came home and set up as a doctor at Truro. In 1781 he moved to London. He brought with him the young Cornish artist John Opie, whose gift for painting he had been the first to see. The two soon quarrelled over a rash bargain to share the artist's gains.
britannica-1911-woodward-john:
John Woodward (1665-1728) was an English naturalist and early geologist, and this 1911 Britannica entry gives his life and work. He was born in Derbyshire and went to London at sixteen, where he studied under a doctor to Charles the Second. In 1692 he became professor of physic at Gresham College, and honours followed.

Visits to Gloucestershire drew his eye to the fossils thick in that county, and he began the great collection tied to his name. His Essay toward a Natural History of the Earth came out in 1695 and set out his views. He showed that the rocky surface of the earth is split into layers and that the shells locked in them began at sea. His ideas on how the rocks formed were quite wrong, the entry says, but his catalogue of rocks, minerals, and fossils was far ahead of its age.
britannica-1911-wycliffe-john:
John Wycliffe is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an English church reformer born in Yorkshire near thirteen twenty. Tales of his birth rest on one old writer and no firm proof. His house held old ties to an Oxford college near their lands.

The entry tells how he rose to head that college for a brief time. A like claim for a post at a rival college is judged a mix up. He took a church living in the shires and left Oxford for a spell. His clash with the church of Rome grew in the years that came next. His call for change made him a mark for praise and blame alike.
caesar-commentaries-mcdevitte-bohn:
Julius Caesar wrote his own campaign reports in crisp third-person Latin. W. A. McDevitte's English translation covers the Gallic War and the Civil War. Caesar presents conquest as orderly, necessary, and brilliantly led.

The Gallic War's seven books trace campaigns across Gaul year by year. The Civil War books then follow his fight against Pompey and the Senate. Caesar's style is famous for clarity, speed, and cold control. Generations of students learned Latin from these pages. Read closely, they also show a master politician shaping his own legend in real time.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambrose-saint:
Ambrose Saint John, Oratorian born in 1815, died at Edgbaston, Birmingham, on 24 May 1875, son of Henry St. John of the Barons St. John of Bletsoe. Westminster School and Christ Church, Oxford, gave him his M.A. and his lifelong friendship with Newman. Curate to Henry Wilberforce at Walmer and East Farleigh, he joined Newman at Littlemore and entered the Church about a month before Newman's October 1845 conversion.

After Maryvale he accompanied Newman to Rome for priestly ordination, then began Birmingham mission work as Oratorians in 1847, moving to Edgbaston in 1852. There he laboured zealously in the Oratory and its famous school, a fine classical scholar and remarkable linguist in Oriental and European tongues. Overwork translating Fessler on infallibility during Newman's Gladstone discussion caused his death, and Newman's Apologia tribute endures.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-epistles-of-s:
The Epistles of Saint John are three canonical books of the New Testament by the Apostle John. For the First Epistle the entry weighs authenticity, canonicity, integrity, author, time and place, and purpose, then turns briefly to the Second and Third. The First Epistle is short, a hundred and five verses in five chapters, and its lateness might suggest no trace in the Apostolic Fathers, yet traces exist.

Polycarp, writing to the Philippians about 110 to 117, says that whoever denies Jesus Christ come in the flesh is Antichrist, an evident echo of First John chapter four. Harnack deems that witness conclusive proof that the First Epistle, and therefore John's Gospel, were written toward the end of Trajan's reign. Polycarp names neither John nor quotes word for word, since the Fathers cited from memory. The phrase come in the flesh also appears in Barnabas about 130.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gospel-of-sai:
The Gospel of Saint John is the last of the four canonical Gospels in the traditional order. Ancient copies sometimes placed it after or even before Matthew. It narrates the life of Jesus from his baptism to his Resurrection and manifestation among his disciples. A Catholic Encyclopedia article treats its contents, peculiarities, authorship, composition, text, genuineness, and importance.

The Gospel falls into a prologue on the Incarnation of the Eternal Word and a first part on the public life to the eve of the Passion. A second part covers the Passion and Resurrection, with a short epilogue on the unrecorded words and works. The author follows historical order with special care for exact time and connection, chronicling the opening ministry almost like a diary, with four successive time marks at the start.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ida-hahn-hahn:
Ida Hahn-Hahn was a countess, convert, and authoress, born in 1805 and dead in 1880. She descended from one of Mecklenburg's wealthiest and most illustrious noble families. But her father, the famous theatrical count, squandered huge sums on drama, reduced the family to straits, and had to be placed under a guardian. Her pious mother's influence likewise repelled her.

The sixteen-year-old girl, due to prepare for confirmation, received a particularly superficial religious upbringing by her own admission. Her general education was just as deficient, leaving gaps she later filled by reading. At twenty-one she married her cousin Friedrich von Hahn, hereditary marshal of Basedow, hence her double name. It was a marriage of convenience, and the entry follows her path from society life to conversion and authorship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johannes-von-:
Johannes von Kuhn was a speculative theologian of the Catholic school at Tubingen, ranked with Staudenmaier as its foremost dogmatist. Born in Wurttemberg in 1806, he studied at Tubingen and was ordained in 1831. He taught New Testament exegesis at Giessen. He moved to Tubingen in 1837, took the chair of dogmatic teaching in 1839, and retired in 1882.

His early work explored the thought of Jacobi. It opposed the destructive tendencies of Strauss in an unfinished Life of Jesus of 1838. His life's work, the Catholic Dogmatics, appeared only in parts. They were an introduction, a treatise on the knowledge, attributes, and unity of God, and a volume on the Trinity. Though never completed, it showed a clear thinker of remarkable gifts for philosophical theology, and his essays in the Tubingen journal carried his influence through the century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prester-john:
Prester John names a legendary Eastern priest-king. A fabled 1122 Rome trip by a Patriarch John of India, with a visit to Callistus II, cannot be the legend's source.  Prester John's first sound mention stands in Otto of Freising's Chronicle, dated 1145.

Otto's source was Hugo, Bishop of Gabala, sent by Raymond of Antioch in 1144 to Pope Eugene III to seek help for Jerusalem. At Viterbo Otto met the Syrian prelate, and there, before the pope, he learned of a John who ruled the Far East as both priest and king. He had with his people turned Nestorian. A few years earlier John had beaten the monarchs of Media and Persia in a three day battle ending in the taking of Ecbatana.  Later lore finds his germ in Jenghiz Khan, the Mongol conqueror who crushed Islam's power in Central Asia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-cyrus-and:
Cyrus and John were martyrs of the Coptic Church. They earned the titles wonderworkers and silverless ones because they cured the sick for nothing. This entry draws mainly on the encomium by Sophronius of Jerusalem. Nothing is known of their birth or youth, and sources disagree over whether John came from Edessa or Alexandria.

Cyrus practised medicine at Alexandria and preached as he healed. Then he fled Diocletian's prefect to a coastal town in Egypt, where he took the monastic habit and lived as an ascetic. John, a high-ranking soldier, sought him out, and the two were later martyred together. Three Roman churches once bore their names, and their feast is 31 January.
doe-osti-2573396-instantaneous-waveform-:
Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/3736, by Yuru Wu, He Yin, and Yilu Liu of the University of Tennessee with Lingwei Zhan, Ben LaRiviere, and Bruce Warmack of the laboratory, is dated December 2024. Its subject is watching the distribution grid's waveforms closely enough to catch misbehavior by solar inverters and other inverter-based resources. Phasor units sample too coarsely to see the fast transients each device can inject.

The team built the practical pieces of a monitoring system instead of streaming every waveform to a server. Event detection comes first: a transient detector, checked in simulation tests and in capture experiments on a real sensor. Data compression follows, squeezing the quiet stretches between events so records stay affordable to send and store. The balance sought is grid visibility at a cost utilities can pay, as rooftop solar and batteries keep multiplying on neighborhood circuits.
doe-osti-3023219-frameworks-algorithms-a:
Kenneth E Jansen of the University of Colorado led the FASTMath SciDAC Institute, and this final report for award DE-SC0021411 covers September 2020 through September 2025. It was submitted March 17, 2026. FASTMath builds frameworks, algorithms, and scalable tools for the mathematics behind huge scientific simulations, especially fusion codes solving very large partial differential equations.

One thrust was in situ data analytics. Simulations now produce data faster than file systems can store it, so the team built ways to compress, visualize, and analyze results while the run is still going. Data-parallel libraries feed samples to machine learning ranks, gather their gradients, and return combined updates. Parts of the work were released as two open source projects.
doe-osti-3029711-frameworks-algorithms-a:
Daniel R. Reynolds of Southern Methodist University files the final report for the university share of the FASTMath SciDAC Institute, under grant DE-SC0021354. The project ran from September 2020 to September 2025, and sat inside the Energy Department SciDAC-5 program. Southern Methodist staff formed part of the Time Integration team, working closely with partner schools and labs. Reynolds is also a core developer of SUNDIALS, the open-source solver library at the heart of the work.

The team pushed three lines: higher-order multirate methods that take mixed step sizes, better step-size control inside those methods, and methods that respect the structure of a problem. They also helped application scientists adopt the new tools. Under this grant, SUNDIALS gained support for complex arithmetic across its Krylov solvers and the rest of the library.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CisnerosRogelio: FBI Name Search Request Form: the bureau's Form 422 routed through the Name Searching Unit and Special File Room - the Rogelio Cisneros request. The bureaucracy's paper trail, complete. A US government document from the archive. Readers will find it rewarding.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DeLoreanJohn_De: A Newsday article dated July 27, 1987 covers a deposition involving car maker John DeLorean and the aging of documents. The piece reports on sworn testimony about how old certain documents really were, a question that turned on tests and expert judgment. The surviving record gives the article's paper, date, and subject, but not its detailed findings, so it stands as a dated news report on that legal fight.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GeorgeJohn_Geor:
An Associated Press report describes an unlikely rescue at sea. The U.S. Coast Guard and two Cuban patrol boats cooperated to save seven Americans from a grounded boat off Cuba. The rescue happened on Christmas, with the two Cold War rivals working the same water for the same crew.

Enemy services rarely share a mission, which is why the wire carried the story. For a few hours, seamanship outranked politics off the Cuban coast. The report preserves that brief cooperation in spare wire-service form, a small human footnote to a hostile decade.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MartinoJohn_Mar:
An FBI memorandum from Miami, dated May 8, 1964, is captioned 'Lee Harvey Oswald — Internal Security — Cuba.' It refers back to a report by Special Agent James J. O'Connor, dated April 4, 1964. O'Connor's subject was John V. Martino of Miami Beach. Martino was an anti-Castro activist whose name runs through the exile politics of those years.

The memo is a link in a chain: one agent's report on an exile figure, folded into the Oswald file by another office. Such cross-references show how the bureau organized a case with thousands of names. A reader can follow the paper from Martino, to O'Connor, to the file where the bureau kept its Oswald material.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-SparrowJohn_Spa: Harold Weisberg, one of the earliest critics of the Warren Commission, wrote a direct reply to John Sparrow. Sparrow had criticized the writing of Weisberg and of Mark Lane, another leading Warren Commission critic. Weisberg answers back and defends their work. The short piece captures the sharp public fights that broke out in the late 1960s between assassination researchers and their reviewers.
historical-papers-part-3-from-volume-vi-:
John Greenleaf Whittier wrote these historical papers, drawn from the sixth volume of his works. Whittier, the Quaker poet, writes here as an essayist of old New England. The set opens with a defence of Daniel O'Connell, the Irish liberator. It answers a Senate speech by Henry Clay from 1839.

Other papers treat James the Second, the border war of 1708, and the great Ipswich fright. Boy captives, Black men in two wars, and the Scottish reformers follow. The Pilgrims, Governor Endicott, and John Winthrop close the list. Readers meet Whittier's moral, plain-spoken take on the colonial past he loved.
king-john:
King John, by William Shakespeare, opens as King John receives Chatillion, an envoy from France. Queen Elinor, Pembroke, Essex, and Salisbury enter with the King. Chatillion has come to speak for the King of France. John asks plainly what France would have with them now. Chatillion greets him, then questions his right to rule England.

Chatillion calls John's majesty borrowed, and Elinor repeats the phrase in surprise. John tells his mother to be silent and hear the embassy. Philip of France, Chatillion says, claims England for Arthur Plantagenet. Arthur is son of John's dead brother Geoffrey, the speech explains. That claim, laid to the island and its lands, drives the scene.
occasional-poems-part-3-from-volume-iv-o:
John Greenleaf Whittier wrote the poems gathered here. They form part three of volume four of his works. Whittier was a well known American poet and abolitionist. The contents list hymns, songs, and poems for public events. Titles include Eva, A Song of Harvest, and Kenoza Lake.

Many poems mark places, seasons, and civic moments in New England. Others honor friends, churches, and national anniversaries. Eva responds to the tale of Uncle Tom's Cabin. The hymns were sung at church openings and school closings. Together they show Whittier as a public, moral voice. Several pieces were written for named days and public gatherings.
personal-poems-i-part-1-from-volume-iv-o: What is hosted here shows only the front matter of Personal Poems I, the title page and contents of part 1 of volume 4 of Whittier's works, with no poems visible. The list begins with A Lament and poems to the memory of Charles B. Storrs and S. Oliver Torrey, then runs through Leggett's Monument, Chalkley Hall, tributes to Channing and Kossuth, and the celebrated Ichabod and The Lost Occasion.
personal-poems-ii-part-2-from-volume-iv-: The hosted sample here shows only the front matter of Personal Poems II, the title page, contents, and a poem heading, with no verse text visible. Part 2 of volume 4 of Whittier's works opens with The Cross and The Hero, then offers tributes to Rantoul, Charles Sumner, and Burns. Memorials of Joseph Sturge and Brown of Ossawatomie follow, and poems for Lydia Maria Child, Garibaldi, Bryant, and Bayard Taylor.
poems-in-wartime-part-4-from-volume-iii-:
John Greenleaf Whittier, the Quaker poet of Massachusetts, speaks in this volume as America's conscience during the Civil War. The contents gather his In War Time group, poems written as the conflict burned: To John C.
